body:
# The lightest human-side gate for version-burn is a two-layer composition

## Summary

[OQ-0040](/open-questions/0040-publish-side-effect-merge-guard/) asks for the *lightest human-side gate*
that catches a publish-on-push merge — the **version-burn** hazard
([current-state](/design/exocortex-current-state/) §Operational hazards #2: merging a feature PR into a
publish-on-push branch cuts a production release, as already happened for ~7 `PrePass.Observability`
versions) — **without standing up CI**, in a **single-maintainer** repo. The constraint is sharp: the
[seam-fences](/design/exocortex-seam-fences/) effect-model fence (#6) would refuse a publish-side-effect
merge target, but **the worker never merges**, so the gate must bind on the *human merge boundary* — the
"autonomy ceiling" fence #6 names — and [RFC-0002](/rfc/0002-personal-agentic-platform/) deliberately
rejects a CI-driven platform, so a GitHub Action is out.

The external evidence — GitHub's own merge-time levers, including two that **post-date this author's
training cutoff** ([A3] required-reviewer GA, Feb 2026; [A4] user-level ruleset bypass, May 2026) —
yields a clear but *honestly partial* answer. **No single no-CI GitHub-native lever both refuses the
wrong-base *semantic* and binds every actor and merge path on every repo visibility.** The lightest
*effective* gate is therefore a **two-layer composition**, with the residual stated rather than hidden:

1. **Binding lever (GitHub-native, repo-settings only — no CI): a branch ruleset on the publish ref that
   requires a pull request before merging, with the maintainer excluded from the bypass list.** "Require
   a pull request before merging" with **zero required approvals** [A2] forces every change to the publish
   ref through a PR — making the *base* visible before the merge click and (bypass disabled) refusing a
   direct or wrong-target push. Crucially, a solo maintainer is an *eligible bypass actor by default*
   [A1][A5], so the gate binds the maintainer's *own* merge only because the May-2026 user-level bypass
   control [A4] lets the ruleset exclude that one user — without it, "require PR" is advisory against its
   own owner.
2. **Wrong-base semantic (client-side, advisory): a `gh pr merge` wrapper that consults the publish-topology
   effect-model** (`resolve_base_ref`'s git-flow-vs-trunk detection via `GITFLOW_INTEGRATION_REF`) and
   refuses a merge whose *base is the publish ref* when the head is not an authorized release/integration
   source. This is the only lever that expresses the *wrong-base* meaning the GitHub repo-settings levers
   cannot — but it binds only the merge path that runs *through it*, not a web-UI click.

This **composes with [OQ-0035](/open-questions/0035-kernel-freeze-merge-time-binding/)** rather than
duplicating it (answering OQ-0040's second `unblock-by`): both want a "require-PR" branch ruleset, but they
**target different refs/paths and demand different bypass postures** — OQ-0035 freezes the *kernel file
paths*; OQ-0040 protects the *publish ref* — so it is one shared *mechanism*, separately *configured*, not
one rule doing two jobs. The disposition is **promote**.

## Motivation

OQ-0040's two `unblock-by` items are (1) a **human-side lever decision** — a `gh pr merge` wrapper that
consults the effect-model, vs. branch protection on publish branches, vs. a review checklist, for a no-CI
single-maintainer repo — and (2) the **composition with OQ-0035** — whether this shares the
branch-protection lever the kernel-freeze residual needs, or is a separate mechanism. Both turn on a
well-documented external surface: *what merge-time levers does GitHub actually offer a solo maintainer who
will not run CI, and which of them binds the maintainer's own merge?*

**The hazard is a wrong-base merge, not a malicious push.** version-burn is the
[seam-fences](/design/exocortex-seam-fences/) *unmodeled side-effect* class: "a publish is a new,
irreducible *effect*… its fence is an effect-model, not a reconciliation" (fence #6). The detection half
already exists — `resolve_base_ref` models git-flow-vs-trunk topology — but "the *worker never merges*, so
this fence binds on the **human merge boundary**, not the worker — note that autonomy ceiling" (fence #6).
So the enforcement locus is not the worker's auto-path (no worker guard can bind a human running
`gh pr merge`); it is the maintainer's merge action. This is the same *wrong-target-around-release-time*
error trunk-based practice warns about: release refs should receive only deliberate, narrow promotions —
"Cherry-picks from the trunk to branch ONLY" [B1] — not the general feature merges that cause a burn.

**A solo maintainer cannot use the obvious lever — required review — as-is.** The first instinct is "require
an approving review on the publish ref." But GitHub enforces that "the author of a PR cannot approve their
changes, requiring at least one other team member to review and approve" [B2]; with a team of one, a
≥1-approval rule is unsatisfiable, forcing the maintainer to either add a second identity or enable admin
bypass — and admin bypass defeats the gate. This is exactly the residual OQ-0035 already flagged ("a
single-maintainer repo may not be able to satisfy a required-review rule on its own PRs"). So required
*review* is not the lightest lever here; it is the heavier escalation.

**Two levers that resolve this post-date the author's knowledge and had to be discovered, not recalled.**
A `/source-recency-probe` against `claude-opus-4-8,2026-01` surfaced two GitHub changes after the cutoff
that are load-bearing: the **required-reviewer rule reached GA on 2026-02-17** and added file/folder
pattern matching "with `!` negation to exclude paths" [A3]; and **repository rulesets gained user-level
bypass on 2026-05-07** — "You can now add individual users as bypass actors on repository-level rulesets"
[A4]. The second is decisive: it is the mechanism that lets a *single* ruleset bind the maintainer's own
merge by *excluding* that user from bypass, which neither the pre-2026 ruleset model nor the legacy
branch-protection "Do not allow bypassing the above settings" toggle [A5] expressed at user granularity.
Any answer authored from training memory alone would have proposed the wrong (review-based) lever and
missed the bypass-exclusion that makes the right one bind.

## Proposal: the lightest *effective* gate is two layers, with a named residual

Design the version-burn gate not as one mechanism but as the **minimal composition** that maximizes the
fraction of the merge surface bound under the no-CI constraint, and *state the merge path no no-CI lever
closes* so the residual is visible, not assumed away.

### Layer 1 — the binding lever: a bypass-disabled "require-PR" ruleset on the publish ref

A **branch ruleset** scoped to the publish ref (the git-flow `main` whose push publishes) with:

- **"Require a pull request before merging", approvals = 0** [A2]. Zero approvals is the load-bearing
  setting: it adds the PR boundary "for visibility… [the team] does not need to approve" [A2], so it is
  satisfiable by a solo maintainer (unlike a ≥1 rule [B2]) while still forcing every change to the publish
  ref through a PR whose *base* is visible before the merge. With pull requests required, a maintainer
  cannot quietly fast-forward a wrong-base branch onto the publish ref.
- **The maintainer excluded from the bypass list.** By default "the restrictions of a branch protection
  rule do not apply to people with admin permissions" [A5], and ruleset bypass is grantable to
  "repository administrator… specific teams or GitHub Apps" [A1] — a solo owner is an eligible bypass
  actor. The May-2026 user-level bypass control [A4] is what lets the ruleset *name and exclude* that one
  user, so the require-PR boundary binds the owner's own merge rather than waving it through. Without [A4],
  Layer 1 is advisory against its author; with it, Layer 1 is binding.

This is GitHub-native, configured entirely in repo settings, runs no workflow, and so honours RFC-0002's
no-CI stance. What it does **not** do is express the *wrong-base semantic*: a PR correctly *opened against
the publish ref as its base* still satisfies "require PR" and merges. Layer 1 refuses the *wrong push* and
makes the base *visible*; it does not by itself refuse a *deliberate-looking but wrong-base* PR merge. That
gap is Layer 2's job.

### Layer 2 — the wrong-base semantic: a client-side effect-model merge wrapper

A `gh pr merge` wrapper (the OQ's named candidate) that, before merging, consults the existing
publish-topology model (`resolve_base_ref` / `GITFLOW_INTEGRATION_REF`) and **refuses when the PR's base is
the publish ref and the head is not an authorized release/integration source** — the
"effect-model on the human merge seam" that [seam-fences](/design/exocortex-seam-fences/) fence #6 names.
This is the only lever that encodes the *meaning* "this merge would burn a version," because GitHub's
repo-settings levers gate *who* and *whether-a-PR*, never *which base is semantically wrong*.

Its honest limit, stated up front: a client wrapper binds **only the merge path that runs through it**.
A maintainer who merges in the GitHub web UI, or types raw `gh pr merge`, bypasses it. Per fence #6's
autonomy-ceiling observation, the gate sits on a *human* action, and no client-side check can bind a human
who chooses a different client. Layer 2 therefore catches the *habitual* wrong-base merge (the maintainer's
muscle-memory CLI path) and is a strong default, but it is **advisory, not enforcing** — which is precisely
why it is paired with Layer 1 rather than offered alone.

### Layer 3 (conditional) — mechanical refusal where the publish trigger is path-localizable

Where the publish trigger is localizable to a file path (a version manifest, a release-workflow file, a
changelog) **and the repo is private or internal**, add a **push ruleset "Restrict file paths"** [A1]
targeting that path. This is the single lever that *mechanically refuses* an offending push on **every
push, regardless of actor**, with no CI. Its constraint is decisive and bounds its applicability: push
rulesets "block pushes to a **private or internal** repository… based on… file and folder paths" [A1] —
they are **not available for public repositories**, and only on Team-tier plans. So Layer 3 is the
strongest refusal *when it applies*, and inapplicable on a public or Free repo — which is why it is
conditional, not the primary lever.

### How the layers add up (and where they do not)

| Merge path | Layer 1 (require-PR ruleset, bypass off) | Layer 2 (effect-model wrapper) | Layer 3 (path push-rule, private only) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Direct push / wrong-base fast-forward to publish ref | **refused** (PR required) | n/a | **refused** if it touches the path |
| Raw `gh pr merge` with publish-ref base | merges (PR exists) | bypassed (not the wrapper) | **refused** if it touches the path |
| Wrapped `gh pr merge` with publish-ref base | merges (PR exists) | **refused** (wrong base) | **refused** if it touches the path |
| Web-UI "Merge" with publish-ref base | merges (PR exists) | bypassed (not a CLI) | **refused** if it touches the path |

The **residual** the no-CI constraint cannot close on a public/Free repo: a maintainer who opens a PR with
the publish ref as base and clicks "Merge" in the web UI is caught by Layer 1 only as *visibility* (the PR
made the base showable) and by neither Layer 2 nor Layer 3. Closing that residual *mechanically* requires
either the required-reviewer rule [A3] (a second identity, heavier and solo-unsatisfiable [B2]),
Layer 3's path push-rule (private/internal only [A1]), or a **topology change** moving the publish trigger
off push-to-branch (e.g. publish-on-protected-tag) — each of which is a deliberate escalation beyond
"lightest," tracked as an open question rather than smuggled into this gate.

### Answering `unblock-by` #2 — composition with OQ-0035

OQ-0035 (kernel-freeze merge-time binding) and OQ-0040 **share the ruleset *mechanism* and differ in every
parameter**:

| Axis | OQ-0035 (kernel freeze) | OQ-0040 (version-burn) |
|---|---|---|
| Protected target | kernel *file paths* (`kernel-baseline.lock` set) | the *publish ref* (git-flow `main`) |
| Rule | require-PR ruleset on those paths — but per [RFC-0012](/rfc/0012-kernel-freeze-merge-time-enforcement/) (which resolves OQ-0035) required review is structurally unreachable for a solo maintainer and the push ruleset is non-binding (plan-gated), so the kernel's *substantive* lever is a worker-side `kernel-baseline.lock` consult, not review-gating | require-PR, 0 approvals, on the ref [A2] |
| Bypass posture | owner retains bypass — but per [RFC-0012](/rfc/0012-kernel-freeze-merge-time-enforcement/) the worker *inherits* the owner's bypass identity, so a path ruleset cannot bind the worker; the kernel lever is the worker-side consult | **exclude the owner** [A4] — the owner *is* the version-burn actor |
| Wrong-base semantic | n/a (any edit to a frozen path is suspect) | needs Layer 2 (base-correctness is the whole question) |

So the honest answer is **composes, does not duplicate**: a maintainer configures *one kind of thing*
(a branch ruleset) twice, with different scopes and bypass lists, and OQ-0040 adds the effect-model wrapper
(Layer 2) that OQ-0035 does not need. Neither OQ's lever subsumes the other; sharing the mechanism is a
reason to resolve them with a *consistent* ruleset vocabulary, not a reason to merge them into one rule.

**Reconciliation with [RFC-0012](/rfc/0012-kernel-freeze-merge-time-enforcement/) (the resolver of OQ-0035).**
The shared thing is the ruleset *vocabulary*, not a claim that a ruleset is the kernel's *binding* lever. On
the publish-ref side (this RFC), the bypass-disabled require-PR ruleset **is** the binding lever for
version-burn. On the kernel side, RFC-0012 concludes the path ruleset is only *accident-resistance* against
unintended human edits — it cannot bind the worker (which inherits the owner's bypass identity) — so the
kernel's binding lever is the worker-side `kernel-baseline.lock` consult. The table above is corrected
accordingly; do not read it as "required review is the kernel rule."

## Alternatives considered

- **Required *approving review* on the publish ref (the obvious lever).** Rejected as *not lightest, and
  solo-unsatisfiable*. "The author of a PR cannot approve their changes" [B2], so a ≥1-approval rule on a
  one-person repo cannot be met without a second identity or admin bypass — and bypass defeats the gate.
  The newly-GA required-reviewer rule [A3] is the *escalation* path (it can scope review to the
  publish-trigger paths with `!` negation), not the lightest default.
- **GitHub Actions environment with required reviewers + "prevent self-review".** Rejected on two grounds.
  It is a *GitHub Actions* construct — the publish job must "reference the environment," and required
  reviewers gate that *workflow job* [A6] — so it is exactly the CI-driven mechanism RFC-0002 rejects.
  And on Free/Pro/Team plans "required reviewers are only available for public repositories" [A6], the
  mirror-image visibility constraint to Layer 3's private-only rule [A1]. Its one attractive feature
  (self-review prevention) is the conceptual model Layer 1 reaches via user-bypass exclusion [A4] without
  standing up a workflow.
- **A `gh pr merge` wrapper *alone* (Layer 2 with no Layer 1).** Rejected as advisory-only. A client-side
  check binds only its own invocation path; the web-UI and raw-CLI merges escape it. It expresses the
  wrong-base semantic no repo-setting can, but as the *sole* gate it is "advisory noise" against any merge
  that doesn't run through it — which is why it is paired with the binding Layer 1, not offered standalone.
- **A `core.hooksPath` pre-merge git hook.** Rejected, consistent with the kernel-freeze decision: the
  hooks path "is shared across ~35 worktrees" (per OQ-0035 and the seam-fences design), so a local hook
  would hijack every worktree and still not bind a web-UI merge. The same rejection OQ-0035 reached.
- **A pre-merge prose checklist / PR template.** Rejected as the floor, not the gate. A template that asks
  "is the base correct?" raises salience but enforces nothing; it is strictly weaker than Layer 1's
  visibility (which the PR boundary already provides) and adds no refusal. Worth keeping as documentation,
  not counted as a gate.
- **Move the publish trigger off push-to-branch (publish-on-protected-tag).** Acknowledged as the
  *mechanically cleanest* answer and deliberately deferred: it converts "guard the merge" into "guard who
  creates the tag," which tag rulesets handle natively and which sidesteps the wrong-base problem entirely.
  But it is a *topology change* to the publish pipeline, not a "lightest gate on the existing topology,"
  so it is out of scope for OQ-0040 and filed as a successor open question.

## Adversarial frames engaged

A `/adversarial-frame` pass over this draft's cited evidence surfaced the following defensible alternatives;
each is engaged.

- **Alternative interpretation — "Layer 1 already binds everything, so Layer 2 is redundant" (grounded
  [A2], [A4], [A5]).** If a bypass-disabled require-PR ruleset refuses unauthorized merges, why add a
  client wrapper? *Engaged; refuted.* Layer 1 gates *whether a PR exists* and *who may bypass* — it does
  **not** inspect the PR's *base*. A PR opened with the publish ref as its base satisfies "require PR" [A2]
  and merges. The wrong-base *semantic* — the actual version-burn cause — is unrepresentable in the
  repo-settings vocabulary, which is why Layer 2 (the effect-model wrapper) is not redundant but
  complementary: it is the only layer that encodes "this base is wrong." Layer 1 binds *every actor* but
  not *the semantic*; Layer 2 encodes *the semantic* but not *every path*. Neither alone is the gate.
- **Alternative weighting — "version-burn is rare and recoverable (releases were deleted), so weight it
  low and a prose checklist suffices" (grounded [B1]).** *Refuted.* The incident already fired ~7 times
  over ~2 weeks (current-state hazard #2), so it is recurrent, not hypothetical; and recovery (deleting
  published releases) is only clean because no consumer had pinned the burned versions — a contingency, not
  a property. Trunk-based practice treats wrong-target-around-release as a discipline error to *prevent*,
  not absorb — release refs take deliberate cherry-picks "ONLY" [B1]. A checklist enforces nothing; the
  cost asymmetry (a one-time ruleset config vs. a production release that *might* have pinned consumers)
  favours the binding lever regardless of frequency.
- **Alternative composition — "compose maximally: require-reviewer rule [A3] on the publish paths *and*
  environment protection [A6] *and* the wrapper — defence in depth" (grounded [A3], [A6]).** *Engaged;
  bounded.* Maximal composition over-shoots the OQ's *lightest* mandate and trips the constraints: the
  required-reviewer rule needs a second identity solo [B2], and environment protection is a CI/Actions
  mechanism RFC-0002 rejects and is public-repo-only on these plans [A6]. The right *ceiling* is stated as
  the escalation ladder (Layer 1 → add Layer 3 if private → add required-reviewer with a bot identity if
  the residual matters), not a simultaneous stack. Defence-in-depth is correct in *shape*; the layers are
  ordered by weight so the maintainer adds only as much as the residual justifies.
- **Alternative interpretation — "the gate must catch the *worker's* merge, and a human-side lever misses
  the actual actor" (grounded in fence #6).** *Engaged; the premise is inverted by the evidence.* The
  worker **never merges** — fence #6's autonomy ceiling — so there is no worker merge to catch; the
  version-burn actor is always the human running `gh pr merge`. The identity question is therefore not
  "worker vs human" but "does the gate bind the *maintainer's own* merge," and the answer is the
  user-bypass exclusion [A4]: without naming and excluding the owner from the bypass list, a solo repo's
  ruleset waves the owner through [A1][A5]. So the human-side framing is correct, and the load-bearing
  detail is owner-bypass exclusion, not worker enforcement.
- **Alternative composition — "this duplicates OQ-0035's lever; resolve them as one rule" (grounded
  [A2], [A3]).** *Engaged; refuted as over-merging.* They share the *mechanism* (a branch ruleset) but
  diverge on target (publish ref vs kernel paths) and rule/bypass posture — see the composition table. On
  the publish ref the require-PR ruleset with the owner excluded from bypass *is* the binding lever; on the
  kernel side, per [RFC-0012](/rfc/0012-kernel-freeze-merge-time-enforcement/), required review is
  structurally unreachable for a solo maintainer and the ruleset is only accident-resistance — the worker
  *inherits* the owner's bypass identity, so a ruleset cannot bind it and the substantive lever is the
  worker-side `kernel-baseline.lock` consult, not review-gating. Collapsing them into one rule would either
  under-protect the publish ref (the kernel ruleset doesn't scope the ref) or misapply the publish rule's
  owner-exclusion to the kernel, where the binding lever is not the ruleset at all. Shared vocabulary,
  separate configuration is the faithful composition.
- **Alternative composition — "for the actual (likely private) burn repos, make Layer 3 the *primary*
  gate, not a conditional add-on" (grounded [A1]).** The push ruleset "Restrict file paths" "block[s]
  pushes to a private or internal repository… based on… file and folder paths" on *every* push regardless
  of actor [A1] — strictly stronger than Layer 1, which lets a wrong-base PR merge through. Since the
  version-burn incident occurred in a PrePass org repo (plausibly private), perhaps Layer 3 should *lead*.
  *Engaged; incorporated as a visibility-conditioned ordering rather than a fixed rank.* Where the publish
  trigger is path-localizable **and** the repo is private/internal, Layer 3 *is* the strongest lever and
  the escalation ladder should put it **first** for that repo — Layer 1 then remains the universal baseline
  that also covers the non-path-localizable trigger and the public-repo case where Layer 3 does not exist
  [A1]. So the layers are not a fixed 1→2→3 rank but a per-repo selection: private + path-localizable →
  lead with Layer 3; public or non-path-localizable → Layer 1 is the only binding floor. This sharpens the
  proposal (the open question on repo visibility is the input that selects the ordering) without changing
  that *some* binding lever always exists.
- **Alternative interpretation — "zero-approval require-PR is 'for visibility' only [A2], so Layer 1 is not
  actually *binding* and the draft overclaims it" (grounded [A2]).** [A2] is explicit that zero approvals
  means a team is "added for visibility, but the team does not need to approve the request" — so what does
  Layer 1 *bind*? *Engaged; the claim is narrowed, not withdrawn.* Layer 1's binding force is **not** the
  approval count (which at zero is indeed visibility-only [A2]); it is the conjunction of *require-a-PR*
  (which blocks a direct or wrong-base push to the publish ref — every change must come through a PR) and
  *bypass-disabled* (which makes that boundary apply to the owner too [A4][A5]). What Layer 1 does **not**
  bind is the maintainer's *unreviewed self-merge of a correctly-based PR* — exactly the residual the
  composition table and Layer 2 address. So "binding" is scoped precisely to the push/boundary, never
  asserted over the merge-approval; the draft's "binding lever" language is correct only in that scoped
  sense, and the frame's caution is folded into the explicit residual rather than left implicit.

## Open questions

- [ ] **Repo visibility of the burn targets.** Layer 3's mechanical refusal is private/internal-only [A1];
  the rejected environment alternative is public-only on these plans [A6]. Which exocortex/PrePass publish
  repos are public vs private decides whether Layer 3 is even available and should be enumerated before
  configuring.
- [ ] **Layer 2 wrapper distribution.** A client wrapper binds only where installed; how is it deployed so
  the maintainer's *default* `gh pr merge` path runs it (shell alias, `gh` extension, PATH shim) without
  becoming a documented-but-not-enforced ritual?
- [ ] **The web-UI residual.** Is the un-closeable web-UI wrong-base merge acceptable as a residual, or
  does it justify the required-reviewer escalation [A3] (with a bot identity) or the publish-on-tag
  topology change? This is the successor OQ.
- [ ] **Bot-identity cost.** If the residual must be closed via required review [A3], is a second
  (bot/CI-app) identity worth standing up for a solo repo, and does that re-introduce a maintenance
  surface RFC-0002's no-CI stance was meant to avoid?

## Risks and mitigations

- **Owner forgets to exclude themselves from bypass, so Layer 1 is silently advisory.** The single most
  likely failure: configuring "require PR" but leaving the owner an eligible bypass actor [A1][A5].
  Mitigation: the configuration step is "require-PR **and** user-bypass exclusion of the owner" [A4] as one
  atomic recipe; a periodic check that the publish ref's ruleset bypass list does not contain the owner.
- **Layer 2 treated as enforcing when it is advisory.** A maintainer who believes the wrapper protects them
  may merge in the web UI and burn a version. Mitigation: document Layer 2 explicitly as advisory and pair
  it with Layer 1's binding boundary; never present the wrapper as the sole gate.
- **Layer 3 assumed available on a public repo.** Push rulesets silently do not exist for public repos [A1];
  a recipe that assumes them would leave a public publish repo ungated. Mitigation: gate Layer 3 on a repo
  visibility check; fall back to Layers 1+2 on public repos and surface the residual.
- **The composition with OQ-0035 drifts into one over-loaded rule.** Mitigation: keep the two rulesets
  separately named and scoped per the composition table; review them together for *vocabulary* consistency,
  not for merging.
- **Post-cutoff features regress or change semantics.** Layers 1 and the escalations lean on 2026 features
  ([A3], [A4]) newer than the author's training. Mitigation: the recipe cites the changelog entries by date
  so a future maintainer can re-verify the feature still behaves as cited before relying on it.

## Related

- [OQ-0040](/open-questions/0040-publish-side-effect-merge-guard/) — the originating open question.
- [OQ-0035](/open-questions/0035-kernel-freeze-merge-time-binding/) — shares the branch-ruleset mechanism;
  this RFC's composition table states how they compose without duplicating.
- [seam-fences](/design/exocortex-seam-fences/) — fence #6 (effect-model on the human merge seam) and its
  autonomy-ceiling caveat, which this RFC operationalises.
- [current-state](/design/exocortex-current-state/) §Operational hazards #2 — the version-burn hazard this
  gate addresses.
- [RFC-0002](/rfc/0002-personal-agentic-platform/) — §Alternatives' no-CI stance, the parent constraint
  every lever here respects.

# How durable is SKILL.md convergence between Claude Code and Cursor?

## The question

`AGENTS.md:27` in dx-aicentral asserts: "Both Claude Code and Cursor have converged on `SKILL.md` as the canonical format for user-invocable workflows." The additive-frontmatter strategy — shared fields + tool-specific fields each tool ignores — collapses if either vendor stops reading the same baseline. The convergence is *current state*, not a contract.

Two sub-questions:
1. How does PrePass detect divergence? (Today: ad-hoc reading of changelogs.)
2. If divergence resumes, what does dx-aicentral do — split skill artifacts, drop a tool, ship a translation layer?

Tool-specific auto-load asymmetry already exists (`.apm/skills/passport-author/references/companion-templates.md:57`: "Cursor only auto-loads AGENTS.md"). The companion-file shape masks this, but the underlying loading semantics aren't shared.

## Why it matters

dx-aicentral's value proposition is single-source skill authoring across both tools. APM ships `target: [claude, cursor]` artifacts as one bundle. Skill authoring assumes additive frontmatter Just Works. A divergence event — without detection or response plan — silently breaks a fraction of consumers on the affected tool.

Vendor decisions are outside PrePass's control. The Agent Skills spec is "silent on versioning" per ADR-0003:34. Cursor has already deprecated `.cursor/commands/` once. The historical base rate for "format convergence holds" is short.

## What's already been considered

- Both tools currently read SKILL.md frontmatter additively (`AGENTS.md:29-45`).
- APM treats them as one distribution target.
- No compatibility matrix exists.
- No contingency plan for divergence is on file.
- [OQ-0026](/open-questions/0026-agent-skills-spec-versioning-silence/) tracks the related spec-silence question.

## What would unblock an RFC

1. Compatibility matrix in `dx-aicentral/references/cross-tool-context-model.md` (or new file) listing shared vs. tool-specific frontmatter fields and loading semantics, dated.
2. Quarterly rhythm to refresh the matrix from current changelogs.
3. Trigger condition: any matrix row that flips from "shared" to "tool-specific" between refreshes opens an RFC reconsidering convergence-as-assumption.

## Quarterly review cadence (added 2026-05-28)

First scheduled review: **2026-08-28** (one quarter from now). Each review: scan Claude Code + Cursor changelogs for SKILL.md frontmatter changes, snapshot the convergence state (shared vs tool-specific fields, loading-semantics asymmetry), and file a one-page note under `content/notes/skill-md-convergence-YYYY-Qn.md`. # Does single-package versioning still fit once we have churn data?

## The question

ADR-0003 in dx-aicentral commits to a single-package release model: "dx-aicentral remains a single-package repo for now" (§Out of scope). All 20 skills + 3 subagents move under one `apm.yml: version` (`apm.yml:2`) + one `.release-please-manifest.json` entry. Consumers pin one line.

The phrasing "for now" is explicit deferral. The question: at what observable churn signal does per-skill versioning become economically interesting?

Specifically: if skill A ships MAJOR bumps weekly while skill B is stable for 6 months, every consumer eats unrelated MAJOR upgrades they don't care about. The version number stops carrying useful signal per skill.

## Why it matters

Single-package versioning is currently friction-minimal for consumers (one pin) and friction-maximal for stability (any skill's MAJOR forces everyone to upgrade). The trade-off is fine at low total skill count and uniform churn, lossy as either grows.

ADR-0003 §Cadence sets a 90-day retro to revisit defaults. This question is one of those candidates.

## What's already been considered

- ADR-0003 §Out of scope explicitly defers the per-skill versioning question.
- No per-skill churn metric is tracked today.
- Release-please's manifest format supports multi-package via `manifest` mode if needed.
- [notes/dx-aicentral-load-bearing-assumptions](/notes/dx-aicentral-load-bearing-assumptions/) row A-0006 holds the working ledger.

## What would unblock an RFC

1. Per-skill commit cadence measured over 90 days post the v1.0.0 cut (skill = `.apm/skills/<name>/` subtree).
2. Compute max-skill-churn / min-skill-churn ratio.
3. Threshold proposal: if ratio > 5× and a single skill drives ≥ 30% of all MAJOR cuts, per-skill versioning is on the table.
4. RFC then weighs the consumer-side cost of N pin lines vs. the stability benefit.

## Related

- [notes/dx-aicentral-load-bearing-assumptions](/notes/dx-aicentral-load-bearing-assumptions/) — assumption A-0006.
- [OQ-0024](/open-questions/0024-stub-forwarder-durability/) — sibling: stub-forwarder pattern under first MAJOR.

# Detect-and-degrade auto-commit for /retro and /write-transcript on protected branches

## Context and problem statement

claude-config PR #84 gave `/retro` and `/write-transcript` an unconditional auto-commit step that pushes to the current branch. When the current branch is the protected `main` of `claude-config`, GitHub's bypass-with-warning behavior accepts the push from the repo owner but emits a non-blocking warning (`"remote: - Changes must be made through a pull request"`) on every push. On 2026-05-27 that warning was misread as a *rejection*, triggering an unnecessary branch+reset "recovery." It also implies the same skills hard-fail for any non-owner account, because non-owners cannot bypass branch protection. [OQ-0032](/open-questions/0032-autocommit-on-protected-main/) holds the question.

## Decision drivers

- **Friction floor.** Retros and transcripts are append-only personal artifacts. Forcing every one through a PR is heavier than the artifact's blast radius warrants.
- **Misread cost.** "Push warning that looks like rejection" trains the operator to either ignore protection signals or run defensive recovery flows that risk data loss.
- **Non-owner correctness.** Any account without bypass rights hard-fails today. The contract should at least be coherent across operators.
- **No-review default.** PR #84 deliberately shipped these auto-commits without a review/CI gate; the platform's stated intent is fire-and-forget for personal artifacts. This ADR does not relitigate that intent.
- **Mechanism cost.** Detecting protected-branch state via `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/branches/<branch>/protection` is a single API call; cacheable for a session.

## Considered options

1. **Direct-push-with-warning (current behavior, PR #84).** Skill pushes; warning surfaces; user ignores.
2. **Branch + auto-PR on a protected branch, always.** Skill creates `<artifact-type>/<slug>` branch, pushes, opens PR.
3. **Detect-and-degrade.** If the current branch is protected, fall back to branch + auto-PR. Otherwise direct-push as today.

## Decision outcome

Chosen: **Option 3 — detect-and-degrade.**

The skill probes branch protection at write time. On a non-protected branch (the existing feature-branch case) behavior is unchanged: direct-push, no PR overhead. On a protected branch the skill creates a side branch named `<artifact-kind>/YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>` (e.g., `retro/2026-05-28-foo`), commits the artifact, pushes the branch, opens a PR via `gh pr create`, and reports the PR URL. The PR is then merged at the operator's convenience or via auto-merge if the repo has it enabled.

The skill never bypasses protection silently. If `gh api` returns 404 (branch unprotected) or 200-with-protection-disabled, direct-push runs. Any other state escalates to branch+PR.

Implementation contract:

- `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/branches/{branch}/protection` runs once per skill invocation; status code drives the branch-or-direct choice.
- **Status mapping (load-bearing — prevents false-positive PR-noise on auth lapses):**
  - `200` with protection enabled → branch + auto-PR path.
  - `404` (branch unprotected) → direct-push path.
  - `200` with protection disabled / null required-checks → direct-push path.
  - `401` / `403` (unauthenticated or insufficient scope) → **direct-push path** with stderr note "branch-protection probe failed (auth); falling back to direct-push." Rationale: assuming protected on auth failure would force a PR for every retro on every machine with a stale `gh auth login`, which is the worst-of-both-worlds outcome.
  - Network failure / 5xx / any other non-200/404 → direct-push path with the same stderr note.
- The misread-warning failure mode is eliminated: on a protected branch (probe-confirmed) the skill *never sees* the warning because it never pushes to protected directly.
- On a non-protected branch (or any probe-failure fallback), the skill prints `verified via git ls-remote` after push, removing the "did it land?" ambiguity that surfaced the original incident.

This ADR is the decision-of-record (research-docs side). The skill-code change lives in `claude-config` and follows as a sibling PR after this ADR merges.

### Consequences

- Positive: works correctly for non-owner accounts (no bypass dependency).
- Positive: protection signals stay meaningful — no normalized "ignore the warning."
- Positive: zero added friction in the common case (feature-branch push unchanged).
- Negative: one PR per retro/transcript on protected branches; PR-noise on `main` of claude-config. Mitigation: enable auto-merge for the `retro/` and `transcript/` branch-name prefixes.
- Negative: one extra `gh api` round-trip per invocation (~50–200 ms). Acceptable given the skill's existing latency budget.
- Neutral: ADR does not change the no-review intent; the auto-merge route preserves it.

## Pros and cons of each option

### Option 1 — Direct-push-with-warning (current)
- Good because zero friction in the common case.
- Bad because trains operator to ignore protection warnings.
- Bad because hard-fails for non-owners.
- Bad because surfaced the 2026-05-27 misread incident in the first place.

### Option 2 — Always branch + auto-PR
- Good because uniform behavior across operators.
- Bad because PR-noise for every personal artifact regardless of branch state.
- Bad because contradicts the lightweight intent of PR #84.

### Option 3 — Detect-and-degrade (chosen)
- Good because preserves the lightweight default where it's safe.
- Good because correct for non-owners and consistent with branch-protection semantics.
- Bad because adds a small probe step + a code path that fires only on protected branches.

- claude-config PR #84 — shipped the auto-commit behavior under question

# Merge-time kernel freeze at single-maintainer scope: accident-resistance, not enforcement-against-will

## Summary

[ADR-0013](/adr/0013-kernel-freeze-discipline/) freezes the exocortex kernel
behind a human-gated lock bump, but two of its enforcement layers do not bind at
merge time: the drift test (`test_kernel_baseline.py`) is local and opt-in, and
`CODEOWNERS` only auto-requests review. [OQ-0035](/open-questions/0035-kernel-freeze-merge-time-binding/)
asks what makes the freeze binding-at-merge, and whether a worker-side guard is
also needed.

**The honest answer reframes the question. At this sharing level — private repos
owned by a single personal user account — no merge-time control can _enforce_ the
freeze against the maintainer's will, because there is no second principal.** A
real merge-time gate requires a key the actor does not hold: an independent
reviewer, an organization owned by someone else, or a third-party check. Here
every candidate collapses to the same will: the maintainer is the repo admin who
configures (and can disable) any ruleset, is the only identity that can approve a
review, and is the owner under whose credentials the worker pushes. Enforcement-
against-will is therefore **not achievable**; the achievable — and worth-having —
goal is **accident-resistance**: making *accidental and automated* kernel drift
hard to land, which is exactly the threat model ADR-0013 names (the worker's
auto-path and unreviewed human slips), not malicious self-override. See
§"Why no merge-time control binds a sole principal."

Within that reframing the disposition is simple. The **one substantive lever** is
a **worker-side `kernel-baseline.lock` consult** on the autonomous path — the only
control that does real work against the actual threat (the worker), because the
worker inherits the maintainer's identity and so is invisible to any GitHub-level
gate [A5]. A **repository push ruleset** restricting the kernel paths [A2][A3] and
**org migration** are **belt-and-suspenders against _accidental_ human edits only**
— useful friction, explicitly *not* enforcement against the maintainer, and (for
the ruleset) gated on an unverified plan tier [A1][B2] besides. The require-review
family is structurally unreachable on a user-owned repo regardless [A4][A6][A7][B1],
and RFC-0002 rejects CI. No CI.

## Motivation

ADR-0013 filed OQ-0035 for two residuals named in its own §Consequences: no
merge-time gate, and a worker with no kernel-lock guard. The "peace property"
asserted by the [exocortex-platform-kernel](/design/exocortex-platform-kernel/)
design doc — a broken brief parks and cannot reach the kernel — is contingent on
closing these. The premise is confirmed empirically: `main` on `research-docs`
currently has a branch-protection record that requires **zero** approvals, does
not require code-owner review, and does not enforce on admins — so the freeze is
detectable-and-advisory, not binding.

The naive expectation is "turn on required review on the kernel paths." That
expectation fails for a single-maintainer user-owned repo, and the non-obvious
finding is that no GitHub require-review primitive is reachable here at all. The
question therefore decomposes by *actor* — accidental human edits, and the
worker's autonomous path — and the answer is a pair of controls covering disjoint
actors, not a single switch.

## External evidence

| Candidate merge-time lever | Status on a private, user-owned repo | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Push ruleset "restrict file paths"** (block edits to the kernel paths via fnmatch, ≤200 entries) | Documented as available on **GitHub Pro** for private repos [A1]; needs no reviewer; owner can be added as an **individual bypass actor** for lock bumps [A5]. **Plan tier unverified on this account; community evidence the gate bites below tier** [B2] | [A1][A2][A3][A5][B2] |
| Branch-protection required review (≥1 approval / code-owner) | Configurable, but **unsatisfiable solo** — author can't self-approve [A4]; required-PR bypass lists are org-only [A6] | [A4][A6][B1] |
| Ruleset required-reviewer-by-team (path-scoped, GA 2026-02-17) | **Unavailable** — needs org teams; "not available on user-owned repositories" | [A2][A7] |
| Required status check (CI runs the drift test) | Available, but rejected by RFC-0002's no-CI stance | — |
| **Worker-side `kernel-baseline.lock` consult** (refuse to dispatch a brief whose diff touches a frozen path) | **Always available** — plan-independent, in-process; the only lever that covers the worker (see §Proposal 1) | — |

Two cross-cutting findings drive the disposition:

1. **The require-review levers all depend on a second reviewer identity** (org
   teams, or a non-author approver) that a single-maintainer user repo lacks
   [A4][A6][A7][B1]. They are not merely awkward here; they are unreachable.
2. **The one no-reviewer GitHub lever has an unverified precondition.** The
   push-ruleset lever is documented as available on private repos with GitHub Pro
   [A1], and the 2026-05-07 user-bypass change [A5] removes the last friction (an
   owner bypassing for an intentional lock bump). But this RFC could not read the
   account's plan tier (the API returns a null plan for the token used), and
   community reports show rulesets silently failing to enforce on private repos
   below the required tier [B2]. The lever may well be available — `research-docs`
   already carries a branch-protection record on a private repo, a paid-tier
   capability — but "may well be" is not a foundation for the peace property.

## Why no merge-time control binds a sole principal

Underneath every row of the table is one fact: **separation of duties is
impossible when all principals are one person.** A merge-time control only
*enforces* a freeze if it interposes a key the acting party does not hold. Walk
the candidates:

- **Push ruleset + owner-bypass.** The maintainer is the bypass actor (so lock
  bumps land) *and* the repository admin who can edit or delete the ruleset
  outright. A control its target can switch off in two clicks is a note-to-self,
  not a gate [A5].
- **Required review.** Satisfaction requires a non-author approver; the sole
  maintainer cannot self-approve [A4], and bypass lists are org-only [A6][B1]. On
  a user-owned repo there is no second approver to interpose [A2][A7].
- **Worker-side consult.** This is code the maintainer wrote, in a process the
  maintainer runs. It guards the maintainer's *agent* (the worker) — useful — but
  it cannot bind the maintainer, and a future regression to that code is authored
  by the same hand it guards.
- **Org migration.** A solo org whose only member/admin is the same person just
  adds steps: that person is the org owner who edits the ruleset and can stand up
  a second account to "approve." The topology changes; the number of independent
  wills does not.

So the strong, GitHub-documented guarantees (team review [A7], org bypass lists
[A6], reliably-enforced private-repo rulesets [B2]) all presuppose an
*organization with a second principal* — exactly what "this level of sharing"
lacks [A2]. Genuine enforcement-against-will needs an **external key-holder**; none
exists here. The freeze is therefore a **Ulysses pact**: the maintainer binding
their *future, distracted, or automated* self, not an adversary. That is a real
and worthwhile property — it is just **accident-resistance**, and naming it
honestly (rather than "binding") is what keeps the peace property from resting on
controls that do not actually hold.

## Proposal

### 1. Worker auto-path: `kernel-baseline.lock` consult — the one substantive lever

Add a `kernel-baseline.lock` consult to the worker's selection/gate path
(`worker-select.py` / `worker-gate-invariants.py`): refuse to select or dispatch
any brief whose diff would touch a frozen kernel file, parking it with a clear
reason.

This is **the primary, not the defense-in-depth, lever**, for two independent
reasons:

- **It is plan-independent.** It is a code guard inside an already-running
  process; it does not depend on GitHub plan tier, on rulesets being enforced on
  a private personal repo [B2], or on any reviewer identity. It is the one control
  guaranteed to exist regardless of how the plan-tier question (§2) resolves.
- **It is the only control that can see the worker.** This is the load-bearing
  composition finding. A push-ruleset bypass actor is an *identity*, not an
  *intent* [A5]: the worker pushes under the maintainer's GitHub credentials, and
  the maintainer is necessarily the ruleset bypass actor (so that intentional lock
  bumps can land) — therefore a kernel-path push ruleset **cannot stop the
  worker**, because the worker inherits the bypass identity. Only an in-process
  consult, ahead of the push, binds the autonomous path.

Additional value: it catches the violation at *selection* time — before a PR is
even opened — a cleaner signal than a push rejection; and it composes with, rather
than duplicates, the existing dx-aicentral-scoped self-mod refusal (which is
target-repo-scoped, not lock-aware). This directly satisfies the design doc's
peace property for the autonomous path, which is precisely the actor the GitHub
lever cannot reach.

*Engaged alternative — could the worker just run under a separate, non-bypass
identity?* Since bypass is granted per individual user [A5], a worker running as a
distinct non-bypass account would be **blocked by the push ruleset like any other
non-bypass actor**, making item 2 redundant with item 1. This is a real option,
and it is rejected for two reasons, not dismissed: (a) it reintroduces a second
automation identity to provision, scope, and rotate — exactly the management cost
the rest of this RFC avoids by leaning on plan-independent in-process guards; and
(b) it still binds the worker only at *push* time, losing item 2's selection-time
signal (the brief never reaches a PR). The separate-identity route is a valid
substitute for teams that already run automation under a dedicated bot; for a
single-maintainer setup the in-process consult is cheaper and earlier.

### 2. Repository push ruleset with owner-bypass — optional belt-and-suspenders against *accidental* edits

Optionally create a **repository-level push ruleset** on each platform repo with a
"restrict file paths" rule [A2][A3] covering the frozen kernel files (mirroring
`kernel-baseline.lock`, ≤200 entries [A2]), with the maintainer as an **individual
bypass actor** [A5] so lock bumps still push. Be precise about what this buys:
because the maintainer is both the bypass actor and the admin who can disable the
rule (§"Why no merge-time control binds a sole principal"), it is **not enforcement
against the maintainer** — it is a speed bump that catches an *accidental* edit
made from a non-bypass context, a stray second automation, or an absent-minded
direct push. That is genuinely useful friction, and it is the entire claim; it does
not, and cannot, bind a determined or distracted owner who chooses to bypass.

It is also **gated on an unverified precondition**: rulesets are documented as
available on private repos with GitHub Pro [A1], but this RFC could not confirm the
account's plan tier, and community evidence shows the enforcement gate biting on
under-tier private repos [B2]. So treat item 2 as opt-in: if cheap and enforced,
add it for the accidental-edit friction; if not, lose nothing that the peace
property depends on, because that property rests entirely on item 1.

### 3. Human-facing layer: keep the drift test + CODEOWNERS

Retain `test_kernel_baseline.py` (local detection) and the auto-requested
CODEOWNERS review as the cheap, human-facing layer. They remain the fast local
pre-check and audit signal; under item 2 (when enforced) they stop being the only
line for human edits, and under item 1 they are complemented for the autonomous
path.

### 4. No CI

None of (1)–(3) is a CI job: (1) is a code guard inside an already-running
process, (2) is a repo setting, (3) is a local test. The RFC-0002 no-CI
constraint holds.

## Alternatives considered

- **Lead with the push ruleset, treat the worker guard as defense-in-depth.**
  This was the earlier framing (the closed PR #78 ordering). Rejected on
  re-verification: it makes the peace property contingent on an *unverified*
  plan-tier precondition [A1][B2], and it misreads the worker case — the ruleset
  cannot see the worker at all because the worker inherits the bypass identity
  [A5]. Leading with the plan-independent, worker-covering control (item 1) is
  strictly more robust.
- **"Require review on the kernel paths."** Rejected as a lever: a user-owned repo
  cannot satisfy required review solo [A4][A6][B1], and the team-scoped ruleset
  reviewer rule is unavailable without an org [A2][A7]. Configuring it would block
  the maintainer's own merges while never being satisfiable — strictly worse than
  doing nothing.
- **Migrate the repos into a GitHub organization.** This deserves more than a
  footnote, because a defensible *alternative weighting* of the same evidence puts
  it first: org migration is the **only** option that simultaneously (a) makes
  team-scoped required review reachable [A7], (b) makes a real second-reviewer
  identity and org bypass lists available [A6], and (c) **removes the unverified
  private-repo ruleset-enforcement doubt entirely** [B2] — the one risk item 2
  cannot retire on a user account. On a pure "what is the most robust binding?"
  weighting, org migration wins. It is **not** the recommendation here for a
  scoped reason: the threat model (§Risks) is accidental/automated drift, not an
  adversary, and item 1 already binds the autonomous path *unconditionally* — so
  the marginal robustness of org migration does not justify its migration cost and
  its conflict with the single-maintainer ergonomics the platform is built around.
  Org migration is therefore the **recommended escalation** if the threat model
  ever hardens (multi-reviewer governance, guaranteed enforcement), not a
  precondition for the freeze to bind today.
- **Bot / GitHub-App second-reviewer identity.** Would make required-review
  satisfiable on a user repo, but introduces an automation identity with
  write/review scope for no benefit over the simpler controls. Rejected.
- **Push ruleset alone, no worker guard.** Rejected as incomplete: even if the
  ruleset is enforced, it cannot bind the worker (bypass-identity inheritance
  [A5]), which is the primary autonomous-drift threat the OQ names.
- **Pre-commit / `core.hooksPath` hook.** Already rejected in the F3 work — the
  hooks path is shared across ~35 worktrees and a hook would hijack all of them.
- **CI required status check.** Closes the gap but contradicts RFC-0002
  §Alternatives; rejected to preserve the no-CI stance.

## Open questions

- [ ] Confirm the account's GitHub plan tier and whether a "restrict file paths"
      push ruleset is **enforced** (not merely created) on a private user-owned
      repo [A1][B2]. This is the one precondition that decides whether item 2 is a
      live second control or deferred.
- [ ] Decide the worker-consult's park-vs-refuse semantics and where it sits
      relative to the existing dx-aicentral-scoped self-mod refusal.

## Risks and mitigations

- **No control here is a hard wall — by construction, not by omission.** At
  single-maintainer scope enforcement-against-will is impossible (§"Why no
  merge-time control binds a sole principal"): the maintainer can bypass the
  ruleset, is the admin who can delete it, and authored the worker guard. The
  honest claim is **accident-resistance** — raising the cost of *accidental and
  automated* drift, the threat model ADR-0013 actually names — not a guarantee
  against a determined or distracted owner. Mitigation: the local drift test
  (item 3) remains the catch-all detector, and §Alternatives names org migration as
  the only path to genuine enforcement (an external second principal) if the threat
  model ever hardens.
- **Plan-tier precondition unverified** [A1][B2]. Mitigation: item 1 is
  plan-independent and carries the peace property alone; item 2's forward action
  includes an explicit enforcement check before it is relied upon.
- **Worker bypass-identity inheritance** [A5]. Mitigation: item 1 is in-process
  and ahead of the push, so it binds the worker regardless of the ruleset.

## Related

- [ADR-0013](/adr/0013-kernel-freeze-discipline/) — the kernel-freeze discipline this RFC's enforcement layer extends.
- [exocortex-platform-kernel](/design/exocortex-platform-kernel/) — the peace property this resolution conditions.

# Is APM a viable long-term distribution mechanism, and what's the contingency?

## The question

ADR-0003 commits dx-aicentral to APM (Microsoft/apm) as the distribution mechanism: exact-tag pins, user-scope deploy via `apm install -g`, `.agent.` infix transform on extraction, release-please integration for tagging. `CLAUDE.md:34` names submodule fallback as "legacy" — explicitly second-class.

Two sub-questions:
1. Is the bet on APM correct over a 2-3 year horizon?
2. If APM freezes, forks, or changes semantics meaningfully, what is dx-aicentral's response — and is it cheap enough to actually execute under deadline pressure?

Single-vendor dependency on Microsoft. No SLA. Known footguns already documented (`references/user-scope/apm-troubleshooting.md` lists 0.8.x hang signature). No "if APM fails" planning document in the repo.

## Why it matters

Every consumer install path goes through APM. Every release-please workflow assumes APM's tag-as-pin semantics. The `/release-notes` skill executes APM-shaped operations. A loss-of-vendor event without prior contingency design is multi-week recovery for the entire AI-tooling rollout.

The "legacy" framing of submodule fallback is a tell — it's documented but not maintained as a true fallback. If APM became unavailable tomorrow, submodule fallback would need re-validation, and several APM-specific design choices (the `.agent.` infix, user-scope deploy paths) would need rewiring.

## What's already been considered

- ADR-0003 §Decision Drivers explicitly weighs APM's tradeoffs and accepts the dependency.
- APM is MIT-licensed and Microsoft-maintained — reasonable but not contractually-backed signal.
- `references/user-scope/apm-troubleshooting.md` documents specific failure modes.
- Submodule fallback path (`CLAUDE.md:34`) exists but is unmaintained.
- No contingency design exists.

## What would unblock an RFC

1. Quarterly APM repo health snapshot: commit cadence, open-issue age, maintainer headcount. Filed in `references/apm-health/YYYY-Qn.md` or similar.
2. One-page contingency design: "If APM is unavailable for 6 months, dx-aicentral migrates to [submodule + setup-script | npm | something else]" with cost estimate.
3. Trigger condition: any health snapshot showing a sustained drop in maintainer engagement opens the RFC.

## Quarterly review cadence (added 2026-05-28)

First scheduled APM-health snapshot: **2026-08-28** (one quarter from now). Each snapshot files at `content/notes/apm-health-YYYY-Qn.md` and captures: commit cadence over the prior quarter, open-issue median age, maintainer headcount, breaking-change incidents. Trigger for the contingency RFC: any snapshot showing a sustained drop in maintainer engagement (commit cadence < 1/month for two consecutive quarters, OR maintainer headcount < 2, OR any breaking-change incident with no published mitigation).

# Skill delivery rigor — definition of "done" per skill

## Overview

This design names the **delivery rigor checklist** every skill in the research-pipeline family must clear before it flips `status: validated` in its brief frontmatter. The runbook [how-to-deliver-a-skill-brief](/runbooks/how-to-deliver-a-skill-brief/) names the procedure; this doc names the *quality bar* the procedure delivers against. Implementation order is [ADR-0004](/adr/0004-research-pipeline-skill-build-order/).

Rigor is not a checklist of vibes. Every item below is a verifiable artifact at a known path with an observable property (file exists, schema validates, metric falls in range, JSON output parses). "Done" means every item below evaluates to PASS.

## Goals and non-goals

**Goals**

- Make "delivered" a falsifiable claim, not an assertion.
- Cover the lifecycle from brief promotion through post-validation drift surveillance.
- Apply across all 7 skill briefs (the 5 pipeline-chain skills + `/criteria-validate` + `/invocation-discipline-lint`). Tier 0–1, Tier 2 (except D2.5) + Tier 4 items apply uniformly; D2.5 (untrusted-input sanitization) gates on external-fetch participation (chain-skills only); D3.4 (failure isolation) gates on chain participation — see per-item notes.
- Avoid recursion: rigor for skills MUST NOT itself be an LLM-judgement surface where the LLM's blind-spot (per [PRIN-0002](/principles/0002-strength-source-equals-blind-spot/)) re-introduces the failure the framework counters.

**Non-goals**

- Replace [SWAF](https://github.com/Wyatt-Rupp_prepass/dx-aicentral/tree/main/references/swaf) (the dx-aicentral Skill Well-Architected rubric) — every D-item below cites its SWAF-ID equivalent where one exists; pipeline-skills inherit SWAF wholesale and add the bias-aware + drift-surveillance extras this doc names. The runbook's step 9b fires `/waf-skill-review` as a parallel structural-quality gate.
- Replace the briefs' per-skill `success_criteria` — this doc names the meta-rigor; per-skill criteria are scoped per-brief.
- Specify how the rigor is measured beyond the runbook's step 9 (`/criteria-validate`) + step 9b (`/waf-skill-review`) + per-skill telemetry — the measurement surfaces exist elsewhere.

## SWAF alignment

Every D-item below is mapped to its SWAF pillar+ID equivalent via a trailing `**SWAF:**` annotation. Three categories:

- **`SWAF: <ID>` (direct)** — D-item enforces the same property as the SWAF criterion. The SWAF score is the authoritative measurement; this D-item is its pipeline-family-specific framing.
- **`SWAF: <ID> (specialization)`** — D-item is a bias-aware or pipeline-specific refinement of the SWAF criterion. SWAF score still applies; D-item adds extra rejection cases the generic SWAF rubric does not name.
- **`SWAF: — (drift extension; see OQ-0028)`** — D-item names a property SWAF does not currently cover. Tier 4 items are all in this bucket; [OQ-0028](/open-questions/0028-swaf-drift-surveillance-pillar/) proposes upstreaming them as a new SWAF pillar or SU extension.

## Definition-of-done checklist

A skill is "done" iff EVERY item below is PASS. Skill briefs may add per-skill items but MUST NOT subtract from this baseline.

### Tier 0 — substrate

- **[D0.1] SKILL.md exists** at `<target_repo>/.apm/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (or `~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`) with valid frontmatter per the Agent Skills standard ([ADR-0003](/adr/0003-extend-agent-skills-as-skill-substrate/)). **SWAF: SU-2** (direct).
- **[D0.2] `allowed-tools` is minimal.** Every entry in the SKILL.md `allowed-tools` field is invoked at least once in the skill body or references/. No "just in case" entries. **SWAF: SE-1 + VA-2** (direct).
- **[D0.3] references/ tree exists if disclosure-first.** Per `feedback_design_disclosure_first` (private memory): new capability = new `references/<topic>.md`, NOT inline expansion of SKILL.md. Triggered when SKILL.md exceeds 200 lines or covers more than one capability surface. **SWAF: PE-1 + PE-2 + SU-5** (direct).
- **[D0.4] Vertical-slice gate passes.** Skill scores ≥40 on SWAF Pillar VA via `/waf-skill-review` before any Tier 2+ item is evaluated — pipeline-chain skills MUST be invocable on their own (with mocked upstream JSON fixture in `evals/`) without another chain-skill being active in the same session. Boundary is explicit: skill body names exactly what it owns vs. what it consumes from its IN-contract. **SWAF: VA-1 + VA-3 + VA-6** (direct; pillar gate per [pillar-va §Gate rule](https://github.com/Wyatt-Rupp_prepass/dx-aicentral/blob/main/references/swaf/pillar-va.md)).

### Tier 1 — contract honor

- **[D1.1] §"Invocation discipline" section in SKILL.md** mirrors the brief's §"Invocation discipline" section verbatim (or evolves it with the brief — if SKILL.md diverges, the brief is updated in the same PR). **Verification:** run `/invocation-discipline-lint` twice — once with the brief as spec, once with the SKILL.md as spec — and diff the extracted IN-required / IN-optional / OUT-bias / OUT-bloat surfaces; non-empty diff means D1.1 FAIL. (Lint's IN-contract accepts a single spec path per invocation; D1.1's mirror check is a two-invocation-plus-diff pattern.) **SWAF: VA-4** (specialization — typed-contract criterion extended with bias-surface enumeration).
- **[D1.2] IN-contract is enforced at invocation parse time.** Skill rejects calls with missing required pointers, unknown optional knobs, or known OUT-bias keys. Reject with a structured error, not silent default. **v1 mechanism:** kwarg-blacklist for bias-encoding patterns (`expected-*`, `focus-*`, `worry-*`, `--expect`, `--baseline`) + per-brief positional-text blocklist derived from the brief's §"Per-skill bias surfaces" list. LLM-judgement second-pass is v2 (acknowledged recursion-turtle per [invocation-discipline-lint brief §Open questions](/notes/invocation-discipline-lint-skill-brief/#open-questions)). **SWAF: SE-4 + CT-5** (direct; argument parsing with type/format validation + structural scope rejection).
- **[D1.3] Inter-skill JSON schemas honored.** If the skill consumes another skill's output (per [skill-invocation-discipline §Inter-skill contracts rule 1](/design/skill-invocation-discipline/#inter-skill-contracts-pipeline-level-discipline)), the input shape is schema-validated at parse time; mismatch = mechanical fail, not silent reformat. **SWAF: VA-4 + RI-2** (direct; typed-handoff + argument-accuracy).
- **[D1.4] Bad/Good invocation example pair from the brief is reproducible.** Running the Good brief produces output structurally matching the brief's declared `output_shape`. Running the Bad brief produces **one of two shapes** depending on the brief's input surface: (a) **kwarg-based briefs** (`/citation-detail-verify`, `/criteria-validate`) — rejection at parse time per D1.2's kwarg-blacklist; (b) **positional-text briefs** (`/load-bearing-fullread`, `/source-recency-probe`, `/adversarial-frame`, `/survey-author`, `/invocation-discipline-lint`) — documented bias-warning telemetry signal (positional strings cannot be argparse-rejected without breaking the legitimate caller-question slot). Both shapes satisfy D1.4; the brief MUST declare which one its Bad-invocation example exercises. **SWAF: RE-3** (specialization — determinism property anchored to the brief's worked example).
- **[D1.5] Constraints are structural, not instructional.** Every "must not", "never", and "reject" claim in SKILL.md is backed by a structural enforcement surface (`allowed-tools` minimization, kwarg-blacklist parser, output-schema validator, path-existence check), not by prose alone. **Verification:** for each prose constraint in SKILL.md, name the enforcing surface in the §"Failure modes" section; constraints with no named enforcement surface FAIL D1.5. The invocation-discipline kwarg-blacklist (D1.2) is the canonical instance of this property; D1.5 generalizes it to every constraint. **SWAF: CT-1** (direct; pillar's defining criterion — "constraints must be enforced in code, not prompts").

### Tier 2 — measurable behavior

- **[D2.1] `success_criteria` is DSL-shaped** per [`/criteria-validate`](/notes/criteria-validate-skill-brief/) primitives (`reduce`, `detect`, `absent`, `compare`). Vibes-criteria fail D2.1 — they're a tier-0 gate, not a tier-2 outcome. **Pre-Stage-2-of-[coordination runbook](/runbooks/how-to-coordinate-skill-family-build/) caveat:** Stage 1's skill (`/citation-detail-verify`) ships before the DSL primitive set locks; its `success_criteria` are written against the provisional v0 DSL declared in the criteria-validate brief and retroactively re-validated at Stage 2 once the DSL lock fires. Provisional-DSL acceptance is bounded to Stage 1 only. **SWAF: VA-4 + RI-6** (specialization — typed criteria narrowed to declarative DSL primitives).
- **[D2.2] `/criteria-validate` PASS on the brief's `success_criteria`** against the brief's declared corpus, with corpus SHA hashed into the validation report for reproducibility. **SWAF: RE-1** (direct; pillar's automated self-verification step).
- **[D2.3] Per-skill eval enrollment.** `<target_repo>/.apm/skills/<name>/evals/expectations.yml` + fixtures shipped per [dx-aicentral-gap-audit #1](/notes/dx-aicentral-gap-audit/). Per-skill Makefile target wires into existing eval harness (`scripts/eval/src/dx_eval/runner.py`). **SWAF: RI-6** (direct; eval coverage criterion).
- **[D2.4] Per-skill eval baseline recorded.** Eval suite run once at delivery; baseline metric (cost_usd, exact-match rate per question, etc.) committed to `<repo>/docs/metrics-branch.md` lineage. **SWAF: RI-6 + CO-1** (direct + specialization; baseline anchors variance acknowledgment).
- **[D2.5] Untrusted-input ingestion is sanitized.** Skills that ingest web pages, PDFs, or any external-fetch content (chain-skills `/citation-detail-verify`, `/load-bearing-fullread`, `/source-recency-probe`, `/adversarial-frame`) MUST parse external content through a sanitizer step that strips active markup, normalizes whitespace, and rejects pages exceeding a documented size cap before the content enters reasoning context. Prompt-injection vectors (e.g., text instructing the LLM to ignore prior context, fabricate citations, or change verdict) MUST be detected with a documented matcher set and either redacted or escalated as UNVERIFIABLE. **Verification:** corpus fixture in `evals/` contains at least 1 poisoned page per skill; eval asserts the skill produces correct verdict despite the injection. **SWAF: CI-1 + SE-4** (direct; external-content sanitization + input validation).
- **[D2.6] Confidence is labeled on every evidence-dependent claim.** Output items carry one of `{verified, partial, self_reported, unverifiable}` derived from the verification surface (D-spec checks per skill). Bare unlabeled claims FAIL D2.6 — "fact without provenance" is the failure mode this gates. The label values harmonize across the chain so `/criteria-validate` can aggregate at the verdict surface (per D3.4). **SWAF: CI-4** (direct; pillar's uncertainty-signaling criterion).

### Tier 3 — operational

- **[D3.1] Trajectory log emitted** per invocation per [skill-invocation-discipline §Inter-skill contracts rule 4](/design/skill-invocation-discipline/#inter-skill-contracts-pipeline-level-discipline) to `~/.claude/telemetry/skill-runs/<name>-<run-id>.json`. Schema: `{skill, run_id, artifact_path, invocation_in_contract_keys[], extractors_called[], cache_hits, cache_misses, corpus_sha, iteration_count_in_pipeline, in_contract_violations[]}`. **SWAF: OE-5 + CI-4** (direct; progress visibility + confidence signaling materialized as per-run telemetry).
- **[D3.2] Failure modes documented in SKILL.md.** Three explicit categories: UNVERIFIABLE handling, fetch failure, partial-success recovery. Each category names a recovery path (skip + log, retry-with-backoff, escalate). **SWAF: OE-2 + RE-2** (direct; prereq validation + no silent error suppression).
- **[D3.3] Idempotency property.** Re-running the skill on the same artifact + same source set produces structurally identical output (modulo fetch-time variance). Property is asserted at D2.3's eval suite via fixture re-run. **SWAF: OE-4 + RE-3** (direct; idempotence + determinism).
- **[D3.4] Failure isolation when chained.** **Chain-participants only** — applies to the 5 pipeline-chain skills (`/citation-detail-verify`, `/load-bearing-fullread`, `/source-recency-probe`, `/adversarial-frame`, `/survey-author`). They MUST NOT halt the chain on UNVERIFIABLE per-citation / per-source failures; downstream skills run on the verifiable subset (per [skill-invocation-discipline §Inter-skill contracts rule 3](/design/skill-invocation-discipline/#inter-skill-contracts-pipeline-level-discipline)). **Out-of-chain skills** (`/criteria-validate`, `/invocation-discipline-lint`) honor a per-spec isolation surface instead: `/criteria-validate` aggregates UNVERIFIABLE at the verdict surface (escalate-to-human only if no FAIL but ≥1 UNVERIFIABLE); `/invocation-discipline-lint` emits per-mode advisory output without aborting parent invocations. The "applies across all 7" claim above accommodates D3.4 by per-skill surface; the *rule* applies to all 7, the *chain* clause applies to 5 of 7. **SWAF: RE-5 + RE-6** (specialization — graceful degradation + partial-output markers extended to chain-aware failure modes).
- **[D3.5] Verify-before-assert at every claim.** All file paths, entity names, URLs, line references, and external-source attributions in the skill's output are confirmed via tools (Glob/Grep/Read/fetch with status check) before being emitted. No claim derives from model memory alone. The skill MUST cite its verification tool call in the trajectory log (D3.1) for each evidence-dependent claim. **SWAF: RI-4 + RI-2** (direct; pillar's central verify-before-assert criterion + argument accuracy). This is what `/citation-detail-verify` *is* as a skill; D3.5 generalizes the property to all 7.

### Tier 4 — drift surveillance

- **[D4.1] Validation re-run on cadence.** `/criteria-validate` re-fires against the brief on at least a quarterly schedule (or per-release for skills tied to a release cycle). Drift in PASS → FAIL or in extracted metric values flagged for re-iteration. **SWAF: —** (drift extension; see [OQ-0028](/open-questions/0028-swaf-drift-surveillance-pillar/)).
- **[D4.2] Skill aging signal queryable.** Skill's last-modified date + last-eval-run date surface in the eval-harness output or an `arch-rover`-class aggregator. Per [dx-aicentral-gap-audit #26](/notes/dx-aicentral-gap-audit/) — invisible aging is undetectable; explicit aging signal is the minimum. **SWAF: —** (drift extension; see [OQ-0028](/open-questions/0028-swaf-drift-surveillance-pillar/)).
- **[D4.3] Failure catalog hooks.** When `/criteria-validate` flips a skill `delivered → failed`, the failure mode is captured in a structured form (not just retro prose) suitable for cross-skill retro analysis. Today: emit to `~/.claude/retros/skill-failures/<skill>-<date>.md` with required frontmatter. Tomorrow: structured per [dx-aicentral-gap-audit #27](/notes/dx-aicentral-gap-audit/). **SWAF: —** (drift extension; see [OQ-0028](/open-questions/0028-swaf-drift-surveillance-pillar/)).

# Should the personal-global aggregator rank/cap/evict the injected memory window, or is add-all acceptable?

## The question

`~/.claude/personal-global.md` is regenerated by `regen-personal-global.py` from every memory entry with `scope: personal-global, stage: active`. Today that render is **add-all**: as of 2026-06-25 it indexes **109 entries** into a 113-line dispatch table that loads into *every* session's context, with **no ranking, no cap, and no eviction**. The schema already carries `cite_count`, `recurrence`, and `last_fired` per entry — the exact fields a ranking/eviction policy would read — but the aggregator uses none of them as a render filter. Entry count is monotonic: 73 at RFC-0004 authoring (2026-05-28) → 109 today.

Should the aggregator rank and cap the *injected* window (and demote low-signal entries to a non-rendered tier), or is rendering the full active set into every session acceptable?

This is the **read-time injection** lever, distinct from the **write-time enforcement** lever that [RFC-0004](/rfc/0004-memory-enforcement-layers/) addresses. RFC-0004 changes how *strongly* a recurring rule is enforced (judgment → skill → hook → CI); it does not reduce — and by promoting more rules, may grow — what gets rendered into context. The two levers compose; neither subsumes the other.

## Why it matters

The cross-session-improvement survey (`content/survey/cross-session-improvement-heuristics.md`, merged #93) rates the **memory-hoarding boundary condition among its most transferable findings**, and supplies the mechanism for *why* an ever-growing rendered blob is a cost even when the right entry is present in it:

- **Lost-in-the-middle [A36]**: retrieval accuracy is U-shaped by position — content in the low-attention middle of a long context is under-used. A 109-row table buries individually-correct rules.
- **Context rot [A37]**: 18 frontier models degrade non-uniformly as input grows, even on trivial retrieval. An add-all blob is a cost independent of whether any entry is wrong.
- **Hoarding compounds [A34]**: add-all retention curves go flat/declining; gating retention on an outcome/quality signal recovers the gains.

The survey's own **Open Question** names exactly this fork as unmeasured: *"write-time gating vs read-time injection as the binding memory lever — which dominates for a cross-session store is unmeasured."* Our aggregator is a pure read-time-injection surface with zero ranking, so it is the cleanest place to test the read-time hypothesis. If read-time injection is the binding lever, no amount of RFC-0004 enforcement-layer promotion fixes the bloat — and may worsen it.

## What's already been considered

- **RFC-0004 (memory enforcement layers)** — the adjacent, orthogonal work. It promotes the ~3 mechanically-checkable high-recurrence rules off Layer-1 advisory text into hooks/CI. That *removes* a handful of rules from "needs to be read every time" by making them fire mechanically — a partial, incidental reduction of the rendered set, but not a ranking/cap policy, and it leaves the ~100 judgment-bound entries rendered in full.
- **OQ-0002 (staleness thresholds per type)** — sibling calibration problem for research-docs doc types; the "what threshold makes the signal noise" framing transfers, but its domain is doc staleness, not memory injection.
- **The schema is ready.** `cite_count` / `recurrence` / `last_fired` already exist and are maintained by `/audit-memory`'s recompute pass; a ranking function is a render-time change, not a schema change.
- **Survey caveats to respect.** (1) The lost-in-the-middle / context-rot studies [A36][A37] are static-context measurements, not write-policy or render-policy tests — they motivate the concern but do not prove a cap helps *here*. (2) `recurrence`-as-keep is the survey's **weakest-evidenced** signal ("principled folklore, not a benchmarked result") — so a ranking function should not lean on recurrence alone; distribution/outcome signals [A14][A34] are better-evidenced.

## What would unblock an RFC

1. **A measurement on this corpus.** Whether memory adherence/retrieval actually degrades as the rendered window grows — the survey's claims are transferred, not validated here. Even a coarse probe (adherence on a held-out rule set with the window at 50 vs 109 entries) would decide whether a cap is worth building.
2. **A ranking function + cap** (or a justified decision that none is needed). If a cap is warranted: what scores an entry's render priority, what the window size is, and how ties break.
3. **A cold-tier mechanism.** A way to keep an entry `active` (cite-discoverable, decay-tracked, re-promotable) while excluding it from the rendered window — so capping is reversible and doesn't silently lose a rule. This is the [A39] "forgetting as a feature" / re-activation-on-citation pattern already present in `/audit-memory` decay, applied to *rendering* rather than *lifecycle*.

## Related

- [RFC-0004](/rfc/0004-memory-enforcement-layers/) — the write-time enforcement-strength lever; this OQ is the orthogonal read-time injection lever.
- [OQ-0002](/open-questions/0002-staleness-thresholds-per-type/) — sibling threshold-calibration problem (doc staleness).
- [OQ-0045](/open-questions/0045-frequency-importance-weighted-decay/) — the write-time decay/forgetting facet; together with this OQ they are the two halves of the survey's "write-time vs read-time" fork.
