- Retro file frontmatter: add `session_id` (synthetic backfill for pre-migration retros). `started_at` was speculative; drop in revision.
- `/note` skill — **already shipped in initial v1**
- `/write-transcript` extension — appends session telemetry JSONL, manages `session_id` cache lifecycle — **already shipped in initial v1**
- `/retro` revert — drop the inbox-disposition / citation-telemetry / hard-fail-check substeps that initial v1 added. `/retro` is reflection + Step 7 finding-emit only.
- `/clarify-inbox` (new) — disposition surface; owns inbox → memory transitions. Hard-fail at >20 items with `--force-triage` escape.
- `/audit-memory` (extended) — adds the citation-telemetry recompute pass over `~/.claude/retros/*.md`; owns `decayed → active` when audit finds new citation.
- `/promote-memory` — manual checklist runbook (unchanged from initial v1)
- One-time backfill: already done in initial v1 — `counted_retros` etc. populated for 20 memories.
- Local Time Machine (or equivalent) handles backup of `~/.claude/`. Single-machine for v1; see § Open chapters.

**Deferred to v1.1+ (after revision lands):**

| Deferred | Why deferred |
|---|---|
| Citation-telemetry snapshot-and-warn | `/audit-memory` v1 does the recompute; v1.1 adds `~/.claude/exocortex/.cite-snapshot.json` and warns on any negative delta to catch retro-file deletion regressions. |

**Deferred to v2 (with dependency justification):**

| Deferred | Why deferred |
|---|---|
| Auto-promotion (no human gate) | Need ≥ 4 weeks of v1 cite_count data to tune the threshold beyond proposed `≥ 3`. |
| Auto-decay | Need v1 telemetry to choose M (weeks). Proposed 12 weeks is a guess. |
| `/work-pattern` reads from memory | Requires `description` to be reliably populated and matched against task descriptions; not all v1 entries have that. |
| Migrate `/retro`, `/write-transcript`, `/note`, `/clarify-inbox`, runbooks to dx-aicentral | Personal↔shared boundary is unresolved; v1's manual `/promote-memory` runs generate the data to settle it. |
| Cross-tool (Cursor) extension | Single-tool focus; Cursor parity is a separate doc. |
| `/promote-memory` / `/audit-memory` as skills (vs runbooks) | Manual flow must stabilize first (≥ 5 runs each without procedural surprises). |
| Append-only citation log | v2 graduation from snapshot-and-warn if retro-deletion regressions actually bite. |
| Scheduled audit notifications | v2 mitigation for `/audit-memory` report-rot. |
| Multi-machine sync | See § Open chapters — explicit v1.5 scope. |

## Failure modes the design assumes won't happen

If any of these fail, the design breaks and needs revisiting:

- **Inbox stays bounded.** `/clarify-inbox` hard-fails at > 20 pending items, with `--force-triage` escape hatch (§ Components → `/clarify-inbox`). Hard-fail is the preventive control; the escape exists so a return-from-vacation backlog isn't a brick.
- **Memory file count stays under ~200.** Schemas, loaders, telemetry assume linear scans are cheap. `decayed` stage exists to keep `active` count low. v1 includes a one-time benchmark of session-load time at 50/100/200 entries (see § Calibration).
- **`/clarify-inbox` runs often enough.** The disposition pipeline assumes a cadence — daily, weekly, end-of-chunk, whichever fits. If it doesn't run, inbox grows toward the hard-fail. Mitigation: `/retro` Step 7's closing report surfaces "inbox has N pending items" when pending count crosses 5.
- **`/audit-memory` runs often enough.** Citation telemetry advances only on audit. If audit doesn't run, promotion candidates don't surface. Mitigation: `/audit-memory` is fast (microseconds at v1 scale); recommend weekly cadence in the runbook.
- **Citation grammar is followed.** Slugs in retros, word-boundary match. § Citation grammar makes this an invariant.
- **`session_id` is set when `/retro` runs.** `recurrence` depends on it. Mitigation: `/write-transcript` generates and caches it; `/retro` reads the cache; synthetic backfill for pre-migration retros.
- **Harness exposes at least the mandatory telemetry fields.** Best-effort fields can be null; mandatory fields are observable to skill code today. Degraded baselines if not.
- **The user actually triages.** v1 partial mitigation: `/retro` Step 7's closing report surfaces "candidates pending" when memories cross threshold. v2 mitigation: scheduled notifications.
- **Stale inbox-emitted findings stay fresh enough.** `/retro` Step 7 emits findings to inbox; `/clarify-inbox` dispositions them. If `/clarify-inbox` is not run for several sessions, findings age — their session context becomes stale (referenced commits may have rolled over). Mitigation: `/audit-memory` flags inbox items older than 14 days; `/clarify-inbox` lists `captured_via: /retro-finding-emit` items first so safety-net items get processed before primary-path captures of similar age.
- **No partial corruption on memory writes.** `/clarify-inbox` writes new memories as atomic file creates (write to `.tmp`, rename). `/audit-memory` writes citation telemetry as per-entry atomic frontmatter updates. A crash mid-write leaves either the old state or the new state, never half — and `/audit-memory`'s recompute is idempotent so re-running after a crash is safe.
- **Retro files are durable.** Citation telemetry is recomputed from `~/.claude/retros/*.md`. If a retro is deleted, citations are lost. Mitigation: tar backup at v1 install; v1.1 snapshot-and-warn detects unexplained `cite_count` drops; v2 may graduate to append-only citation log.

## Open chapters

Calibration choices left unresolved. Each carries the evidence that would resolve it.

- [ ] **Concrete promotion thresholds.** Proposed v1: `cite_count ≥ 3` AND `recurrence ≥ 2`. Resolution: tune after 4-6 weeks of v1 data. Evidence: distribution of `cite_count` across entries. See § Calibration for sensitivity.
- [ ] **Concrete decay timeout M.** Proposed v1: 12 weeks. Resolution: tune from `last_fired` distribution. Evidence: median inter-fire interval; M should sit in a gap of the distribution if one exists.
- [ ] **Hard-fail threshold N for inbox-backlog.** Proposed v1: 20 items. Resolution: tune from `inbox_items_captured` per chunk distribution. Evidence: how often `/note` invocations cluster; if a typical chunk produces 5-10 captures, N=20 covers two chunks' worth.
- [ ] **Soft cap on memory file count.** Proposed v1: 200. Resolution: one-time session-load benchmark at 50/100/200/400 entries. Evidence: where Claude Code's auto-load latency starts to bite.
- [ ] **Should `/work-pattern` consume personal memory?** Deferred to v2. Evidence: usage data showing `/work-pattern` runs that *could* have benefited from a memory-driven pattern the fixed corpus missed.
- [ ] **Should personal-layer skills migrate to dx-aicentral?** Resolution after `/promote-memory` and `/audit-memory` runbooks have stabilized (≥ 5 runs each without procedural surprises). Evidence: whether other PrePass engineers express interest in the same flow.
- [ ] **Multi-machine sync (v1.5).** v1 is explicitly single-machine. v1.5 introduces dotfiles-repo-based sync if/when a second machine enters the workflow. Resolution trigger: a second machine becomes load-bearing for daily work. Evidence: usage attempts from another host. The minimal-rework requirement means the v1.5 design must preserve v1's filesystem layout and not introduce conflict-resolution machinery — single-writer assumption at any moment.

### Resolved inline (formerly v1-blocking)

- **Backup.** Resolved: Local Time Machine (or platform-equivalent: `rsync` snapshot, OS backup) covers `~/.claude/` including inbox, retros, memory, and telemetry. No special pathway. The dotfiles-repo-for-skills question (whether `~/.claude/skills/` should be in version control independently of backup) is folded into the "Should personal-layer skills migrate to dx-aicentral?" open chapter and the "Multi-machine sync (v1.5)" open chapter — both downstream of v1's manual-flow experience.
- **What is the disposition surface called?** Resolved: `/clarify-inbox`. GTD's verb for "process the inbox into the right home" — one word, lineage, unambiguous.
- **Where does citation telemetry live?** Resolved: `/audit-memory`, as a recompute-from-retros pass. Not live increment; not a hook.

## Calibration

The proposed thresholds (`cite_count ≥ 3`, `recurrence ≥ 2`, `M = 12 weeks`, hard-fail N=20, soft cap 200 files) are deliberately conservative starting points.

**`cite_count ≥ 3`.** At current scale (18 lesson memories, 3 retros, per-retro dedupe), **n=0 entries meet this** — the proposed threshold would lock out promotion entirely at v1 ship time. `feedback_design_disclosure_first` (cite_count=2) is the closest. Lowering to 2 yields 1 candidate; lowering to 1 yields 6. The threshold is purely speculative until 4-6 weeks of post-v1 retro activity produces a distribution. (Note: `feedback_design_disclosure_first` was previously promoted to `dx-aicentral` under v0 ad-hoc judgment, not via the v1 threshold — promotion conversion rate is therefore undefined at v1 ship.)

**`recurrence ≥ 2`.** Guards against "cited 3 times in one retro." With session = single `/retro` invocation, this and `cite_count ≥ 3` together require: ≥ 2 distinct retros AND ≥ 3 total citations. In practice often the same constraint; v2 may consolidate.

**M = 12 weeks.** Invented; roughly one quarter. Quarterly-recurring lessons (annual review patterns) would decay-and-re-fire — wasting telemetry events but not damaging anything. Lower (6w) → seasonal patterns decay; higher (24w) → store accumulates dead weight, partially countered by `/audit-memory` aggressive flagging at active > 100.

**Hard-fail N = 20 inbox items.** Invented. Approximately two chunks' worth of captures at observed `/note` rate (estimate: 5-10 per chunk). Lower (10) → triggers mid-week if note rate is bursty; higher (40) → real backlog before the alarm fires. The `--force-triage` escape ensures the threshold doesn't brick a returning-from-vacation workflow.

**Soft cap 200 memory files.** No empirical basis. v1 includes a one-time benchmark of session-load time at 50/100/200/400 entries to set a real threshold.

Every threshold is a v2-tuning target. v1's job is to capture the data that decides them.

## Operational concerns

- **Deployment:** edit files in `~/.claude/`. No build step. `/note`, `/audit-memory` runbook, `/promote-memory` runbook ship as new files under `~/.claude/skills/` and `~/.claude/exocortex/runbooks/` respectively.
- **Observability:** session telemetry JSONL is the primary surface. Weekly `awk`/`jq` one-liner derives baseline metrics; no dashboard in v1.
- **Backup:** Local Time Machine (or equivalent) covers `~/.claude/`. Telemetry, inbox, retros, and memory all included.
- **Privacy:** session telemetry includes `repo` and `branch` basenames only — no secrets. Token *counts* only, never token contents. Inbox bodies and retro bodies are private; they live only on the local machine until a `/promote-memory` flow opts in to PR them.
- **Tampering / integrity:** frontmatter is hand-editable. `/audit-memory` validates invariants on every run (`cite_count = len(counted_retros)`, `recurrence = len(counted_sessions)`, `cite_count ≥ recurrence`, `last_fired ≤ today`, stage-field consistency).
- **Partial-retro failure recovery:** retro file writes are atomic (tmp + rename). Memory frontmatter writes are per-entry atomic. Citation telemetry is idempotent via recompute-from-scratch — `/audit-memory` re-runs the full citation pass on every invocation, so an interrupted run leaves the next run unaffected. `/retro` does not write citation fields in v1.1. No transactional spanning.
- **`~/.claude/.current-session` lifecycle:** populated by `/write-transcript` or `/retro` on fallback; consulted by both. Cleared by either on session-close after the telemetry line writes successfully. Stale value at session-start is overwritten with a warning, never trusted.

# What staleness thresholds drive the loose-ends sweep per doc type?

## The question

The [loose-ends methodology](/design/methodology-unfinished-work/) flags docs as *stale* when their `date` (or `last benchmark run`, or `rehearsal-evidence` commit date) exceeds a per-type threshold. The thresholds themselves are unset. Picking them wrong is the single most likely way the audit becomes noise on day 30 — too tight and authors learn to ignore the report; too loose and stale work never surfaces.

Open variants:

- Should ADR stale thresholds depend on `status` (proposed = 14 days; accepted = never; superseded = never; deprecated = never)?
- Should RFC `draft` stale at 14 days but `review` stale at 7?
- Benchmark staleness should follow declared `cadence` (weekly = 14d window; per-release = N/A); is anything stricter useful?
- Runbook `rehearsal-evidence` cadence — quarterly? per-release? defer to the runbook's own `cadence:`?
- Principle orphan window (zero ADR citations) — 90 days? 180? Until cited at least once?

## Why it matters

The thresholds are the audit's only time-decay signal. Every other category (Pending, Dangling, Orphan, Undefined) is state-based and binary. Staleness is the slider that controls report volume; mis-calibrated it becomes the load-bearing source of false positives or silent rot.

This question blocks the audit script (`bin/audit-loose-ends.py`) from shipping with the *stale* category enabled. The script can ship without that category and add it later — but doing so means stale rot accumulates terminally until calibration lands.

## What's already been considered

- Industry analogues (ADR-tooling, Open Source RFC repos) typically don't enforce time-decay on accepted artifacts. Drafts decay at 7–30 days in most public RFC processes.
- The Hugo `enableGitInfo` setting exposes git-last-modified per page, which the audit could read instead of frontmatter `date` — but then *edits* reset the timer, masking real staleness. Frontmatter `date` (authoring date) is the right signal; staleness is "we haven't *thought* about this since X," not "we haven't touched the bytes since X."

## What would unblock an RFC

1. 20+ real docs in the corpus, so calibration has signal not just assumption.
2. One run of the audit with provisional thresholds across all categories; observe false-positive rate and adjust.
3. Agreement on whether thresholds are per-type-constant or per-doc-overridable (frontmatter `staleness-override:`).

Once those exist, write an RFC proposing the table.

## Related

- [methodology-unfinished-work](/design/methodology-unfinished-work/) — defines the *stale* category as a load-bearing audit signal.
- [how-to-audit-loose-ends](/runbooks/how-to-audit-loose-ends/) — the runbook this question gates.

# How to deliver a skill brief through openspec to validated

## When to run this

A skill brief lives at `content/notes/<name>-skill-brief.md` (or another repo's equivalent) and is ready to advance from "briefed, unbuilt" to "delivered, validated." This runbook covers the full lifecycle gates from [RFC-0002 §Pipeline gates](/rfc/0002-personal-agentic-platform/#pipeline-gates).

Trigger: maturity gate passes (frontmatter `evidence`, `success_criteria`, `target_repo` populated and non-empty) AND build order ([ADR-0004](/adr/0004-research-pipeline-skill-build-order/)) says this skill is next.

## Pre-conditions

- `openspec` CLI v1.3+ installed (`brew install openspec` or equivalent; verify via `openspec --version`).
- Brief's `target_repo` has an `openspec/` directory initialized (`openspec init` if absent).
- Brief's `success_criteria` is DSL-shaped per [`/criteria-validate`](/notes/criteria-validate-skill-brief/) primitive set (`reduce`, `detect`, `absent`, `compare`) — vibes-criteria fail this gate.
- Brief's §"Invocation discipline" section is present (framework link + IN-required + IN-optional + OUT-bias + OUT-bloat + dominant-concern + Bad/Good example pair).
- Author or worker has `gh` authenticated against `target_repo`.

## Steps

### 1. Promote brief to spec scaffold

```bash
# In target_repo (where the skill will live, e.g., ~/.claude or dx-aicentral)
openspec change new <skill-name>-skill --from-brief <path-to-brief>
```

If `/brief-to-spec` skill exists, invoke it instead: `/brief-to-spec <path-to-brief>`. Produces `openspec/changes/<skill-name>-skill/` with `proposal.md`, `tasks.md`, and `specs/` scaffold.

Brief's `promoted_to: openspec://<repo>/<change-name>` populates atomically. Brief status flips `ready-for-spec → promoted`.

### 2. Author the design

Edit `openspec/changes/<skill-name>-skill/design.md` from the brief's §Scope + §Pipeline composition + §Invocation discipline. The design names:

- Concrete file layout under `~/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/` (or equivalent target).
- SKILL.md `allowed-tools` enumeration.
- references/ tree (if disclosure-first per [`feedback_design_disclosure_first`](file:///Users/wyatt.rupp/.claude/projects/-Users-wyatt-rupp-dx-prepass-meta-repos-dx-aicentral/memory/feedback_design_disclosure_first.md)).
- evals/ scaffold for per-skill eval-harness enrollment ([dx-aicentral-gap-audit #1](/notes/dx-aicentral-gap-audit/)).
- Inter-skill JSON schemas it consumes / produces per [skill-invocation-discipline §Inter-skill contracts](/design/skill-invocation-discipline/).

### 3. Validate the spec

```bash
cd <target_repo>
openspec validate changes/<skill-name>-skill
```

Validation MUST pass before tasks generation. If validation fails, fix the spec — never bypass.

### 4. Generate tasks

```bash
openspec tasks generate changes/<skill-name>-skill
```

Produces `tasks.md` with dependency-ordered concrete units. Review tasks against the brief's §Scope to catch under-specification (gaps) or over-specification (off-scope rabbit-holes) per [`delegation-briefing`](file:///Users/wyatt.rupp/.claude/skills/work-pattern/references/patterns/delegation-briefing.md).

### 5. Implement

Three patterns acceptable, per task risk class:

- **Direct implementation in this session** (low-risk tasks, mechanical work): run tasks inline.
- **`/openspec-apply-change` (or `/opsx:apply`) skill** (medium-risk): the skill drives tasks sequentially with status updates.
- **Worker fire** (continuous worker per RFC-0002): worker picks the change and runs one task per fire.

Each task MUST be verified, not just checked, before its checkbox flips per [`feedback_openspec_checkboxes_can_lie`](file:///Users/wyatt.rupp/.claude/projects/-Users-wyatt-rupp-dx-prepass-meta-repos-dx-aicentral/memory/feedback_openspec_checkboxes_can_lie.md).

### 6. Draft PR

```bash
gh pr create --base main --head <branch> --title "<conventional-commit-title>" --body-file <body-path>
```

Body MUST include:

- Summary (3–5 bullets covering scope of skill + its pipeline position).
- Files-changed table.
- **Test plan** that PRIN-0001-routes typed assertions (the file:line citations [`run-pr-test-plan`](file:///Users/wyatt.rupp/.claude/skills/run-pr-test-plan/SKILL.md) can mechanically verify).

### 7. Review + merge

- For dx-aicentral target_repo: `@PrePass/architecture` gate per [`dx-aicentral-gap-audit`](/notes/dx-aicentral-gap-audit/) Pillar D.
- For ~/.claude target_repo: maintainer self-review with at least one critic-subagent pass per `feedback_critic_rounds_before_code`.
- Auto-merge on green if risk-class is low (`docs`, audit hygiene, validation rerun) per [RFC-0002 §Decision-rights split](/rfc/0002-personal-agentic-platform/#decision-rights-split).

### 8. Archive the openspec change

```bash
openspec archive changes/<skill-name>-skill
```

Brief frontmatter `status: promoted → delivered` flips atomically. Brief becomes input to the validation gate.

### 9. Validate against success_criteria

```bash
/criteria-validate --brief <path-to-brief>
```

`/criteria-validate` reads the brief's `success_criteria`, runs the DSL primitives against the declared corpus, writes `validation-report.md`, and flips `status: delivered → validated` (PASS) or `delivered → failed` (FAIL).

FAIL reopens the brief at `status: failed` with reason; iterate. PASS is the terminal state.

### 9b. SWAF structural-quality gate

```bash
/waf-skill-review <target_repo>/.apm/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md
```

Run in parallel with step 9 (no ordering dependency — they measure orthogonal properties). `/criteria-validate` answers "did the skill produce the declared outcome?"; `/waf-skill-review` answers "is the skill structurally well-architected?" Per the [SWAF (Skill Well-Architected) rubric in dx-aicentral](https://github.com/Wyatt-Rupp_prepass/dx-aicentral/tree/main/references/swaf), it scores 10 pillars (VA / OE / SE / RE / PE / CO / SU / RI / CT / CI) with risk-weighted question sets and writes a scorecard to `<target_repo>/.waf/skill/<skill-name>-scorecard-YYYY-MM-DD.md`.

**Promotion thresholds** (per [skill-delivery-rigor §SWAF alignment](/design/skill-delivery-rigor/#swaf-alignment)):

| Tier | Pillar(s) | Minimum score | Failure action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tier 0 gate | VA (Vertical Slice + Autonomy) | ≥40 | Hard fail. Brief reopens at `status: failed`; revise scope to make skill stand alone. No Tier 1+ scoring proceeds. Matches SWAF's own gate rule per [pillar-va §Gate rule](https://github.com/Wyatt-Rupp_prepass/dx-aicentral/blob/main/references/swaf/pillar-va.md). |
| Tier 1 | OE, SE, RE, PE, CO, SU | ≥60 each | Soft fail per pillar: scorecard names the criterion; brief annotates the gap; iterate or accept via explicit waiver in the brief's `success_criteria` (waiver text MUST cite which SWAF ID is being deferred and why). |
| Tier 2 | RI, CT, CI | ≥50 each | Same soft-fail mechanic as Tier 1, but Tier 2 pillars are 1.5× weight per SWAF — accepted waivers MUST be tracked in the brief's `outstanding_quality_debt` field. |

Both step 9 PASS AND step 9b clearance (all Tier 0 + Tier 1 thresholds met, Tier 2 met or waiver tracked) are required for `status: delivered → validated`. Either failing reopens the brief at `failed`.

### 10. Cross-cutting hygiene (each step)

- **Trajectory log** (per [skill-invocation-discipline §Inter-skill contracts rule 4](/design/skill-invocation-discipline/#inter-skill-contracts-pipeline-level-discipline)) written at every skill invocation in the lifecycle.
- **Invocation-discipline lint** (per [`/invocation-discipline-lint`](/notes/invocation-discipline-lint-skill-brief/)) gates every invocation in `enforce` mode once the lint ships.
- **Per-skill eval enrollment** at step 2's design — author `evals/expectations.yml` + fixtures BEFORE implementation, not after.

## Expected outcome

- Skill lives at `<target_repo>/.apm/skills/<skill-name>/` (or `~/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/`) with SKILL.md + references/ + evals/.
- Brief frontmatter shows `status: validated`, `promoted_to: openspec://...`, `validated_by: <path-to-validation-report>`, `waf_scorecard: <path-to-scorecard>`.
- Validation report + SWAF scorecard archived alongside brief.
- `/criteria-validate` re-run on cadence (next scheduled validation drift check per [skill-invocation-discipline §Inter-skill contracts rule 4](/design/skill-invocation-discipline/#inter-skill-contracts-pipeline-level-discipline)).

## Rollback

Reversal per-step:

- **Step 8 archive → revert:** `openspec unarchive <change-name>`. Brief flips back to `promoted`. PR remains merged; archive is the openspec-state, not git-state.
- **Step 7 merge → revert:** `gh pr revert <pr-number>` produces a revert PR. Brief flips back to `delivered` → re-iterate from step 5 or 6 as the rollback PR lands.
- **Step 9 validation FAIL:** brief reopens at `failed`; revise (re-author scope, fix bug, re-enter at step 5); validation re-runs.
- **Step 1 promotion regret:** `openspec drop changes/<name>-skill` + manually flip brief `status: promoted → drafting`. Rare; brief that survives the maturity gate but later proves un-implementable is a design failure, not a rollback target — typically supersede with a successor brief rather than drop.

# Guard the zsh `git show "$ref:$path"` footgun with a shell-free verdict-path invariant and a shared safe helper, not a blanket lint

## Summary

OQ-0037 names [current-state](/design/exocortex-current-state/) operational hazard #10: in zsh, an unbraced parameter reference followed by `:` and a path can have the text after the colon parsed as a history-style *modifier* rather than literal path text, silently mangling the path passed to `git show <rev>:<path>` [A2], [A3]. An empty/wrong read on an `absent`/count check is a **silent false-PASS** — a correctness failure in the verdict path, not an annoyance. But the trusted verdict path does **not** use the shell form: it shells out via Python `subprocess` list-args (`criteria-verdict.py:352`, `["git","-C",root,"show",f"{ref}:{rel}"]`), which never invokes a shell, so the footgun cannot fire there today. The live question is therefore preventative: **given no current exposure, is a machine guard warranted for the future shell-script / interactive surface, and if so — lint, shared helper, or convention?**

This RFC proposes a **layered, proportionate guard** grounded in cross-domain external precedent and one empirical finding produced while resolving the OQ:

1. **Ratify the secure-by-construction invariant** that the trusted verdict path stays shell-free (Python list-args), exactly the defense OWASP prescribes over fragile escaping [A6] and Bandit prescribes over shell invocation [A5]. This is the primary guard and it is *already true* — the RFC makes it an explicit, enforceable property rather than an implicit accident.
2. **Provide a shared `git_show_file(ref, path)` helper** for any shell surface that must shell out, using a form empirically verified safe (`git show "$ref" -- "$path"`, or brace-delimited `"${ref}:${path}"`). This is the Pit-of-Success move [B2]: make the easy path the safe path.
3. **Reserve linting for a narrow, advisory backstop** — never a blanket fatal rule. A blanket lint fails on three counts: ShellCheck does not support zsh at all [A4]; the false-positive budget for trusted checks is under 10% [B1] and a noisy rule erodes adoption [A1]; and — decisively — the exact pattern the hazard ledger names as unsafe (`"$ref:$path"`) is empirically *safe*, while the form that actually bites is different (see Motivation). A lint keyed to the documented pattern would be maximally miscalibrated.

## Motivation

The "use the safe `git show` form" rule is prose-only — a `documented-but-not-enforced` hazard. The failure mode is severe and quiet: a mangled path yields an empty read, an `absent`/count check passes vacuously, and a verdict is wrong with no error. That is precisely the class of bug a machine guard exists to prevent.

But the warrant must be weighed honestly, because the hot path is not exposed. Two facts reshape the decision:

**Fact 1 — the footgun fires non-interactively, in scripts, not only in interactive shells.** This is *not* the well-known `!`-triggered history expansion (which is interactive-only and disabled by `setopt NO_BANG_HIST`). It is the colon-*modifier* expansion, which the zsh manual documents applies to ordinary parameter substitution: "the colon modifiers described in Modifiers in History Expansion can be applied: for example, `${i:s/foo/bar/}` performs string substitution on the expansion of parameter `$i`" [A2]. The modifiers include `:e` (extension), `:h` (head/dirname), `:t` (tail/basename), `:r` (root) [A2]. Because this is parameter-expansion behavior, **it fires in `zsh -f -c` (no rc files, non-interactive)** — so a future shell *script*, not just an interactive paste, is genuinely exposed. That raises the warrant above "interactive-only nuisance."

**Fact 2 — the exact unsafe form is narrower than the hazard ledger states, and this inverts a naive lint.** Resolving this OQ included running the forms through `zsh -f -c` directly. The result refines the ledger's framing:

| Form | Result | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `git show "$ref:$path"` (variable : variable) | **safe** | the `$` after `:` is not a modifier letter, so `:` stays literal |
| `git show "$ref:${path}"` (variable : braced) | **safe** | same — `$` after `:` |
| `git show "${ref}:$path"` (braced : variable) | **safe** | `}` closes the parameter name before `:` |
| `git show "$ref" -- "$path"` (separated) | **safe** | `:` never appears adjacent to a parameter |
| `git show "$ref:exocortex"` (variable : literal `e…`) | **mangled** → `xocortex` | `:e` extension modifier binds to `$ref`, then literal text follows |
| `git show "$ref:head.md"` (variable : literal `h…`) | **mangled** → `originead.md` | `:h` head modifier binds to `$ref` |

The form the ledger calls unsafe — `git show "$ref:$path"` with both as variables — is in fact **safe**, because the character immediately after the colon is `$`, not a modifier letter. The form that actually bites is `git show "$ref:<literal path beginning with a modifier letter>"`. A lint keyed to the documented `"$ref:$path"` pattern would therefore **false-positive on the safe variable form and false-negative on the dangerous literal form** — the worst possible calibration. (This refines, not contradicts, the OQ: the hazard is real; its precise trigger is just narrower than the prose states, and the safe forms the OQ already recommends — brace-delimited or `--`-separated — remain correct.)

Together these say: a guard is warranted (Fact 1), but a pattern-matching lint is the *weakest* mechanism (Fact 2), which is why the proposal leads with secure-by-construction.

## Proposal

### Primary guard — the shell-free verdict-path invariant

The strongest defense against an injection/quoting footgun is to make the dangerous construct *structurally absent*, not to detect it after the fact. This is the universal lesson across two independent precedents:

- **OWASP** ranks parameterized queries as the primary defense and explicitly downgrades escaping/filtering — the lint analog — as fragile: "This methodology is fragile compared to other defenses, and we CANNOT guarantee that this option will prevent all SQL injections in all situations" [A6]. The recommended path is to bind values, not to police strings.
- **Bandit** flags shell-spawning subprocess calls and recommends functions that do not spawn a shell, because "This type of subprocess invocation is dangerous as it is vulnerable to various shell injection attacks" [A5]. Critically, Bandit rates the risk *highest* exactly when "the string is computed using Python's string manipulation or formatting operations" [A5] — i.e. an f-string. The verdict path's `f"{ref}:{rel}"` *is* such an f-string, but it is passed as a **list argument to `subprocess` with no shell**, so the f-string is interpolated by Python, never re-parsed by a shell. That is the secure-by-construction property in action.

So the verdict path is *already* on the right side of both precedents. This RFC ratifies that as an explicit invariant: **the trusted verdict path (and any criteria-extraction path whose output gates a PASS/FAIL) MUST shell out via `subprocess` list-args, never via a shell string.** Making the invariant explicit converts an implicit, accidental safety into a property a reviewer (or a future check) can assert against — which is the whole point of moving a rule from prose to a guard.

Taken to its limit, the invariant says **eliminate the shell surface wherever feasible**, not merely guard it: the strongest form of the OWASP "rewrite to parameterized" lesson [A6] and the Pit-of-Success "make the wrong thing structurally hard" lesson [B2] is to make the inline shell `git show` form *unrepresentable* in the protected surface by routing all git reads through Python list-args. Where a path can be written in Python, it should be — there is then no shell construct to get wrong. The helper below exists only for the irreducible shell surface where elimination is not feasible.

### Secondary guard — a shared safe `git_show_file` helper

For shell surfaces that legitimately must exist (interactive verification one-liners, future shell tooling), provide one shared helper that every such call routes through, e.g.:

```bash
# safe in zsh and bash: '--' separates the rev from the pathspec, so ':' never
# sits adjacent to a parameter reference and no modifier can bind.
git_show_file() { git show "$1" -- "$2"; }
```

The `--` form is the gitrevisions-documented way to name a path while disambiguating it from a revision [A3], and it is empirically safe in the trigger matrix above. This is the Pit-of-Success principle [B2]: "we want our customers to simply fall into winning practices … To the extent that we make it easy to get into trouble we fail." A safe helper makes the obvious call the safe call.

### Tertiary guard — a narrow, advisory lint as a regression backstop

A lint is the *last* layer, not the first, and it is **advisory, not fatal**. Its only job is to catch a *regression* — a future commit that reintroduces an inline shell `git show "$x:…"` in a protected surface — not to police every shell script in the tree. Three constraints bound it:

1. **It must be a custom or zsh-specific rule, because the dominant linter cannot help.** ShellCheck "does not support scripts written for other shells like Zsh, Csh, Tcsh or PowerShell" [A4]; forcing `--shell=bash` reports bash semantics, missing the zsh-specific modifier behavior entirely. Three practical mechanisms exist: a project-local `grep`/CI check; a custom Semgrep rule, which exists precisely to "Identify secure coding violations" [A7]; or a dedicated zsh analyzer — `zsh-lint`, "a standalone Go-based semantic analyzer for Zsh" that "parses Zsh scripts and reports greppable static-analysis diagnostics" [B3]. A recency probe (post-2026-01) confirmed ShellCheck shipped no zsh support through its latest release and surfaced `zsh-lint` as the one zsh-aware option — but it is early-stage (single release, low adoption) and does not document a check for this specific colon-modifier pattern, so it cannot today be relied on as the backstop without verifying and likely contributing the rule upstream. The mechanism choice is deferred (Open Questions).
2. **It must be precise to the *real* trigger (Fact 2), not the documented one.** The pattern is an unbraced `$name` immediately followed by `:` and then a modifier letter (or another unbraced `$`, which though safe is a smell). It must NOT flag the safe `"${name}:…"` or `… -- …` forms. Matching the ledger's `"$ref:$path"` verbatim would invert the tool's value.
3. **It runs under a false-positive budget.** Trusted checks need under 10% effective false positives or developers route around them [B1]; false positives "killed off" a Google tool's code-review integration [A1], whose success ultimately came from issues "fixed by engineers, by their own choice" [A1]. An advisory, low-noise backstop respects that budget; a blanket fatal rule on a non-exposed path would not.

## Alternatives considered

- **Convention only — document the safe form, accept the risk.** Defensible *today* because the hot path is shell-free, and it costs nothing. Rejected as the sole disposition because it is exactly the `documented-but-not-enforced` pattern the OQ flags: it relies on every future script author remembering a subtle, zsh-specific rule (made subtler by Fact 2), and the failure is a silent false-PASS. The shell-free invariant costs little and is assertable, so "do nothing" leaves cheap, durable safety on the table.
- **Blanket fatal lint on every `git show "$…:…"`.** Rejected. It cannot ride on ShellCheck [A4]; a custom blanket rule would false-positive on the safe variable/braced forms and miss the dangerous literal form (Fact 2); and a noisy trusted check erodes adoption below the <10%-FP bar [A1], [B1]. Linting is demoted to an advisory backstop, not removed.
- **Shared helper as the *only* guard.** Rejected as insufficient on its own. Unlike a type system or a parameterized-query API [A6], a shell helper does not *prevent* the unsafe inline form — both can coexist, and adoption is a discipline, not a guarantee (the known limit of the Pit-of-Success framing [B2], which is about steering, not forbidding). The helper is necessary but must be paired with the shell-free invariant (so the hot path has *no* shell to get wrong) and the advisory lint (so regressions in protected surfaces surface).
- **Rewrite the verdict path to add escaping (`shlex.quote`) around a shell call.** Rejected: it moves the trusted path *toward* the shell — the wrong direction. Both precedents [A5], [A6] say remove the shell, not escape into it; the path is already shell-free and should stay that way.

## Adversarial frames engaged

`/adversarial-frame` and the three identity/composition holes flagged for this question are each engaged here:

- **"If the hot path is already shell-free, does a guard protect anything real, or is it warn-fatigue on a non-path?"** *Engaged.* The guard's primary value is the **invariant** (Proposal §Primary), which protects a real and currently-true property at near-zero cost and gives a reviewer something to assert against. The lint — the part with warn-fatigue risk — is explicitly demoted to advisory *because* the live path is not exposed. We do not add a noisy blanket rule to a non-path; that is the alternative we reject.
- **"Does a lint fire on safe usages (false positives) or miss the unsafe form (false negatives)?"** *Engaged head-on, and it is the strongest finding in this RFC.* The empirical trigger matrix (Fact 2) shows the documented `"$ref:$path"` pattern is *safe* and the dangerous form is the literal-suffix variant. A naive lint would be maximally miscalibrated; the tertiary-guard constraints require the lint to target the real trigger and stay advisory under a false-positive budget [A1], [B1].
- **"Shared helper vs lint — does the helper actually get adopted, or does the unsafe inline form persist alongside it?"** *Engaged.* A helper steers but does not forbid [B2]; the inline form can persist. That is exactly why the helper is not the sole guard — it is paired with the shell-free invariant (the hot path has no shell at all, so there is nothing to adopt or forget) and the advisory regression lint (which flags inline shell git-show in the protected surfaces). The layering exists *because* no single mechanism is sufficient.

A second `/adversarial-frame` pass over this RFC's own cited evidence surfaced three further defensible alternatives; each is engaged:

- **Alternative interpretation — the false-positive budget is calibrated for Google-scale code review, not a single-author correctness gate (grounded [A1], [B1]).** The "<10% effective false positives" bar [B1] and "fixed by engineers, by their own choice" trust model [A1] describe a high-volume, multi-developer review-warning stream; this exocortex is a single-author repo where the check guards a verdict-path correctness invariant, not a review queue. *Incorporated, narrowing.* At single-author scale the tolerance for a few false positives on a rarely-touched path is higher, which slightly *raises* the case for even a blunt lint — so the FP-budget magnitude is NOT the decisive argument here. The decisive argument is **precision-impossibility** (Fact 2): a lint keyed to the documented pattern is inverted regardless of how many false positives are tolerable. The tertiary-guard rationale therefore leads with precision, not FP-volume; the FP-budget [A1], [B1] is a secondary, scale-dependent consideration.
- **Alternative weighting — weight defense-in-depth higher; Bandit flags broadly then tiers, implying flag-don't-suppress (grounded [A5]).** Bandit reports an issue even for low-risk shell calls, merely *tiering* severity [A5]; re-weighted, that argues a lint deserves co-primary status, not tertiary. *Refuted with reason.* Bandit's flag-everything model is viable because `shell=True` is an unambiguous, exactly-detectable construct with near-zero false positives. The zsh colon-modifier footgun is the opposite (Fact 2): the safe and dangerous forms differ only by whether a literal modifier-letter follows the colon, across quoting variants — not precisely pattern-detectable. So [A5]'s flag-broadly model transfers only to unambiguously-detectable constructs; importing it to an undetectable one reproduces the very warn-fatigue [A1], [B1] it exists to avoid. The part of [A5] that *does* transfer — "use functions that do not spawn a shell" — is exactly the primary invariant, which is why the invariant, not the lint, carries the defense-in-depth weight.
- **Alternative composition — the cited evidence composes into a stronger claim: eliminate the shell surface, not merely guard it (grounded [A6], [B2]).** [A6] prescribes *rewriting* to parameterized queries (removing the dangerous channel), and [B2] prescribes making the wrong thing structurally hard; composed maximally, this says do not offer a shell helper *alongside* a persisting unsafe form — make the inline shell form unrepresentable by routing all git reads through Python list-args. *Incorporated as the ceiling, bounded by feasibility.* Where the shell surface CAN be eliminated — the hot path, and any tooling that can be written in Python — it SHOULD be; that is the invariant taken to its limit, and it is the strongest available guard. The helper exists only for the irreducible shell surface (interactive one-liners, shell-only tooling) where elimination is not feasible and steering [B2] is the best lever. This tightens the Proposal from "invariant + helper" to "eliminate where feasible; helper only for the irreducible remainder."

## Open questions

- [ ] **Protected-surface boundary.** Which directories/files count as "trusted/verdict-adjacent" for the invariant and the advisory lint's scope? `criteria-verdict.py` and the worker preflight are in; what about ad-hoc `scripts/`? Drawing the boundary too wide reinflates the false-positive cost [B1].
- [ ] **Lint mechanism — grep vs Semgrep vs `zsh-lint`.** A `grep -E` CI check is dependency-free but coarse; a custom Semgrep rule [A7] is more precise but adds a tool; `zsh-lint` [B3] is the only zsh-aware analyzer but is early-stage and does not yet document this pattern, so adopting it means verifying coverage and likely upstreaming the rule. Given the rule is advisory and zsh-specific, does a tight `grep` suffice, or is one of the heavier tools warranted?
- [ ] **Helper home.** Where does `git_show_file` live so both shell scripts and interactive use can source it without a sibling-path dependency (per the umbrella's "submodules point up, never sideways" rule)?
- [ ] **Bash parity.** The mangling is zsh-specific, but the helper and invariant should be shell-agnostic. Confirm the `--` form is equally safe and idiomatic under bash (it is, but worth a one-line test in the implementing change).

## Risks and mitigations

- **Over-scoping the lint reinflates warn-fatigue.** Mitigated by keeping the lint advisory, narrow to the real trigger (Fact 2), and bounded to the protected surface — staying under the <10% effective-FP bar [A1], [B1]. If the rule cannot be made precise enough, ship only the invariant + helper and drop the lint.
- **The invariant is asserted but not mechanically checked.** Ratifying "the verdict path is shell-free" in prose is itself a `documented-but-not-enforced` step unless paired with a check. Mitigation: the advisory lint's regression role *is* that check for the inline-shell case; a complementary check that the verdict path imports `subprocess` and never sets `shell=True` (Bandit-style [A5]) can enforce the Python side.
- **Helper non-adoption.** A helper that no one sources changes nothing [B2]. Mitigated by the layering: the hot path needs no helper (it is shell-free), and the advisory lint nudges new shell call sites toward the helper. The helper's value is for the long tail of legitimate shell usage, where steering is the best available lever.
- **Mischaracterizing the zsh mechanism.** Mitigated by grounding every behavioral claim in a `zsh -f -c` run (the trigger matrix) plus the zsh manual [A2] and gitrevisions [A3], rather than restating folklore — the OQ's own framing was refined by exactly this exercise.

# Does the 5-skill research-pipeline decomposition outperform a single fat "verify-all" skill on the same artifact corpus?

## The question

The 7-skill research-pipeline family ([ADR-0004](/adr/0004-research-pipeline-skill-build-order/)) decomposes verification into 5 chain-skills (`/citation-detail-verify`, `/load-bearing-fullread`, `/source-recency-probe`, `/adversarial-frame`, `/survey-author`) plus the meta-validator `/criteria-validate` plus the enforcer `/invocation-discipline-lint`. The multi-agent design pattern asks: "did decomposition produce something a single agent couldn't?" This question stays open until empirically answered against a single fat baseline.

## Why it matters

Without an empirical baseline, the decomposition is justified by reasoning ("each skill's bias surface is narrower, schemas compose, fetch cache amortizes") but not by measurement. If a single `/verify-all` skill turns out to produce comparable output at lower coordination cost, the chain's overhead is unjustified. If decomposition wins, the win-margin sets expectations for future similar families.

This is also load-bearing for whether to invest in [RFC-0002](/rfc/0002-personal-agentic-platform/)'s continuous-worker contract pattern for *all* skill families or only families where decomposition empirically pays back.

## What's already been considered

- [skill-invocation-discipline §Open questions](/design/skill-invocation-discipline/#open-questions) names the baseline as a deferred question.
- [ADR-0004 §Single-skill baseline](/adr/0004-research-pipeline-skill-build-order/#single-skill-baseline-deferred-to-oq-0027) gates the baseline build on at least 3 chain-skills shipping (so the comparison has substrate).
- [how-to-coordinate-skill-family-build §Stage 5 step 4](/runbooks/how-to-coordinate-skill-family-build/) names the benchmark as either a sibling PR after Stage 5 OR a deferred OQ routed here.
- The work-pattern `multi-agent` priming source explicitly raises "single-agent baseline" as the hardest test for any agent-decomposition design.

## What would unblock an RFC

A single benchmarking PR that:

1. Defines `/verify-all` (single skill: same artifact input, fetches sources, runs all framing probes + recency check + adversarial framing + citation-detail check in one LLM pass per artifact).
2. Runs both surfaces against the same ≥3 artifacts from this repo. Records: token cost (input + output), wall-clock, output-quality scored against a frozen expected-findings list per artifact (compiled by hand pre-experiment to avoid post-hoc bias).
3. Cost compare + quality compare table. Pre-commit the success criterion: "Decomposition wins iff (quality > baseline+ε) AND (cost < baseline × k) for declared ε, k."
4. Discussion: where decomposition won, where it didn't, and why. Specifically: did the schema-locked inter-skill handoffs catch contract drift the single-agent baseline tolerated? Did the per-skill IN-contract reject more bias inputs than the single skill's monolithic IN-contract did?

Once measured, this OQ promotes to either an ADR (if decomposition wins) or an ADR + sibling ADR-0004 revision (if decomposition loses or breaks even).

## State as of 2026-05-28

The first `unblock-by` item ("≥3 of the 5 chain-skills shipped") is **met**: all 5 chain skills (`/citation-detail-verify`, `/load-bearing-fullread`, `/source-recency-probe`, `/adversarial-frame`, `/survey-author`) plus the meta-validator (`/criteria-validate`) and enforcer (`/invocation-discipline-lint`) are listed in the available skills surface. The substrate for a meaningful benchmark exists.

What remains is the actual benchmark work — building `/verify-all` as a single-fat baseline, running both surfaces against ≥3 artifacts, and capturing cost + output-quality metrics. That work has not begun. The OQ stays `open` because the missing piece is the measurement itself, not skill availability.

The natural next surface is an **eval brief** (`content/evals/`) or a **benchmark** (`content/benchmarks/`) that runs the comparison and publishes the table. Either would carry this OQ in its `decided-from:` chain.

# How to enhance an existing RFC

## When to run this

An existing RFC in `draft` or `review` status has a load-bearing section that needs updating because:

- One of its §Open questions resolved (sibling ADR landed; needs back-reference).
- Prior-art assumptions in §Motivation or §Alternatives changed (a published source contradicts a cited claim; a new sibling RFC reframes the tradeoff).
- §Proposal needs a new subsection — a thread that was un-named at original-author time now has a coherent shape.
- §Motivation needs additional failure modes to justify §Proposal's scope (reviewers said "the proposal is over-built for what §Motivation describes").
- A fact correction: typo, outdated link, misattributed citation.

NOT for: changing the core question. If the core question is wrong, withdraw the RFC and open a new one per `content/rfc/_index.md` Conventions — "If discussion reveals the question is wrong, withdraw the RFC and open a new one — don't mutate it past recognition."

Exemplars: RFC-0002's two follow-up edits — commit `b6576b1` (bumped citation references from ADR-0001 to ADR-0002 after a sibling ADR shipped) and `fc5d64d` (committed to `dx-arch-meta` as the umbrella name after OQ-0014 resolved). Both are additive, both cite the resolving artifact, both kept the RFC's §Summary central claim untouched.

## Pre-conditions

- **The RFC is in `draft` or `review` status.** `awk '/^status:/{print $2; exit}' content/rfc/<file>`. Halt if `accepted` or `rejected` — see §Out-of-scope below.
- **The mutation does NOT change §Summary's central claim.** §Summary is the gate of RFC identity. If it needs rewriting, that's a new RFC.
- **The mutation cites a stable anchor.** A merged sibling PR, a resolved OQ, a published source, an accepted ADR, OR a **navigation back-reference** — a sibling artifact that already cites the RFC (via frontmatter `related-rfcs:` / `decided-from:` or prose pointer) where the reciprocal pointer is missing from the RFC's §Related. Navigation back-refs are valid even when the sibling artifact is itself `status: proposed` / `draft`; the cited target's existence on disk is the anchor, not its acceptance state. Mutations without any citable anchor are usually just author indecision and should marinate in notes first.

## Out of scope

- **Accepted RFCs.** They are historical artifacts. Mutate the corresponding ADR (via [how-to-promote-rfc-to-adr](/runbooks/how-to-promote-rfc-to-adr/) when it exists) instead. If the ADR is also already landed, open a new RFC to revise; don't edit the old one.
- **Rejected RFCs.** Same as accepted — historical. The lesson lives in `## Alternatives considered` of any future RFC that revisits the territory.
- **Withdrawn RFCs.** Forked into a new RFC; the old one stays as lineage anchor (the new RFC names the withdrawn predecessor in its §Related section — RFC frontmatter has no `originating-rfc:` field).
- **Core-question changes.** Withdraw + new RFC, not enhance.

## Steps

### 1. Confirm the RFC is mutable

```bash
awk '/^status:/{print $2; exit}' content/rfc/NNNN-<slug>.md
```

If output is `draft` or `review`, proceed. If `accepted`, `rejected`, or `withdrawn`, halt and read §Out of scope.

### 2. Identify the section being changed

§Summary, §Motivation, §Proposal/<subsection>, §Alternatives, §Open questions, §Risks, §Steering signals, §Related. Note which is being changed AND which are NOT — silent ripples across sections are the most common drift mode. An edit to one section often implies an edit to another that cites the same fact.

If the enhancement is in §Proposal but cites a new fact that §Motivation also relies on, both sections change. Plan the ripple before authoring.

**Iterative-loop enhancements: catalog shortfalls upfront, split into non-deferred and deferred.** When the enhancement is a multi-fix sweep (loop-shaped, more than one shortfall), write a scratch catalog (e.g., `/tmp/<RFC-NNNN-slug>-shortfalls.md`) with two sub-lists:

- **Non-deferred** — each row has a stable anchor (per §Pre-conditions) and gets fixed this PR. One commit per row.
- **Deferred** — each row has no stable anchor yet, OR its anchor requires work outside the current PR's scope (e.g., the resolving ADR is still `proposed`, or the unblock-by items haven't landed). Each deferred row names the missing anchor in one sentence so a future PR can resurrect it.

The deferred sub-list is not a punt; it is the explicit surface that prevents the loop from running too long or from forcing a shortfall through with a weak anchor. Empirical anchor: this runbook's PR #28 deferred 4 shortfall classes (5 unanchored OQ promotions, OQ-0012 pending ADR-0004 acceptance, OQ-0014 pending its own `unblock-by`, §Motivation pre-proposal-framing) and that bookkeeping let the loop terminate cleanly.

### 3. Cut a fresh branch from origin/main

```bash
git fetch origin main
git switch -c claude/enhance-rfc-NNNN-<topic> origin/main
```

Fresh-branch-from-origin/main is the cheapest insurance against mid-session integration drift; a stale base branch will accept the enhancement and then surprise-conflict at merge time.

Branch-name convention is `claude/enhance-rfc-NNNN-<topic>` (verb-first: action-then-target). Earlier runbook revisions used the legacy `claude/rfc-NNNN-enhance-<topic>` shape (target-then-action); the verb-first form aligns with how downstream tooling and user-prompt invocations actually name iterative-loop branches and is the form used by this runbook's own PR #28 (`claude/enhance-rfc-0002-personal-agentic-platform`).

### 4. Make the edit

Discipline (in this order of preference):

- **Append-only.** A new subsection beats rewriting an existing one. Future readers should be able to trace the RFC's evolution by reading top-to-bottom. RFC-0002's enhancement commits both added clauses rather than rewriting existing ones.
- **Surgical correction.** When existing prose must change (a typo, a fact correction, an outdated link), the diff is tight (one line per fact) and the commit message names the anchor (e.g., "post-ADR-0002 reference bump").
- **Avoid silent rewrites.** If a paragraph's meaning shifts even slightly, the commit message states what shifted and why — never edit prose meaning without a rationale line in the commit body.
- **Status field stays untouched** unless the enhancement IS the explicit transition (`draft → review`, `review → accepted | rejected | withdrawn`).

### 5. Ripple-propagate if the mutation touches multiple sections

After editing the primary section AND BEFORE staging the commit (`git add`), grep the whole RFC for the pre-edit phrasing:

```bash
git diff content/rfc/NNNN-<slug>.md | grep -E "^-"  # pre-edit lines
grep -n "<key-phrase-from-pre-edit>" content/rfc/NNNN-<slug>.md
```

Hits in other sections MUST be updated in the same commit. Silent cross-section drift is a repeat finding from critic passes — running the propagation check is the cheap insurance. Empirical anchor: this runbook's PR #28 shortfall #5 caught a second `stage 2-4 implementation` hit in §Related only because the grep ran post-edit-pre-commit; without it the surgical correction in §Motivation would have shipped stale phrasing in §Related.

### 6. Update §Open questions if the enhancement closes one

OQ valid status states per [content/open-questions/_index.md](../open-questions/_index.md) are `open | parked | promoted | dropped`. There is no `resolved` state — when an OQ is closed by an ADR or RFC landing, it transitions to `promoted` with `promoted-to: ADR-NNNN` (or `RFC-NNNN`).

Two valid conventions for the RFC-side bookkeeping; pick one per RFC and don't mix:

- **Inline checkbox + ADR back-reference**: `- [x] OQ-NNNN — promoted to ADR-NNNN`.
- **OQ doc carries the status**: leave the §Open questions bullet unchecked; flip the OQ-NNNN doc's frontmatter to `status: promoted` with `promoted-to: ADR-NNNN`. The RFC's §Open questions list is the index, not the source of truth.

The second is preferred when the resolution chain is non-trivial (multiple OQs promoted into one ADR; one OQ promoted to a sibling RFC; etc.).

**A third pattern is allowed and orthogonal to the two above: an empirical-state inline note on an OQ bullet whose underlying question is partially answered but not yet promotable** (the OQ doc stays `status: open` per its own `unblock-by` list). RFC-0002 §Open questions OQ-0014 demonstrates the shape: bullet stays unchecked, inline note records the empirical update plus the residual `unblock-by` items keeping it open. Don't confuse this with promotion — it is a status-of-the-world annotation, not a state transition. Use it sparingly; when the empirical answer crosses the OQ's `unblock-by` threshold, flip to the inline-checkbox or OQ-doc-status convention.

### 7. Critic gate — 1 read-only subagent

For enhancements smaller than a full §Proposal subsection, one critic is sufficient (from-scratch authoring needs two; enhancements are bounded scope).

Critic invariants to check:

- **§Summary central claim preserved.** The enhancement does NOT change what the RFC is fundamentally proposing. If §Summary needs rewriting, halt and convert to a withdrawal + new RFC.
- **Append-only vs surgical-correction discipline followed.** If existing prose changed, the commit body cites why.
- **Cross-section propagation complete.** No stale pre-edit phrasing survives in other sections.
- **§Open questions bookkeeping consistent.** Either inline-checkbox or OQ-doc-status convention; not both (the §6 empirical-state inline-note pattern is orthogonal and does not count as "mixing").
- **Frontmatter schema honored.** No invented fields. The valid RFC frontmatter keys are exactly: `id`, `title`, `status`, `date`, `author`, `tags`, `resolves-to`, `originating-oq`, `build`. Critic must flag any `parent-rfc:` / `originating-rfc:` / `resolved-by:` introduced. Valid OQ status values are `open | parked | promoted | dropped`; flag any `status: resolved` introduced on the RFC or any cited OQ doc.
- **Anchor cited in commit body.** The stable anchor (per §Pre-conditions, including the navigation-back-ref class) is named in the commit message; "felt right" is not an anchor.

### 8. If the enhancement IS the `accepted` transition

This is a different shape than other enhancements. The enhancement PR MUST also include:

- The new ADR at `content/adr/NNNN-<slug>.md` with `decided-from: [RFC-NNNN]`.
- The RFC's `status: accepted` and `resolves-to: ADR-NNNN`.
- §Open questions all resolved (each bullet either closed inline or its OQ-NNNN doc flipped to `resolved`).

If any §Open question is still open at acceptance time, either resolve it first (separate PR) or defer the acceptance transition. Accepting with open questions strands them — they have no parent RFC to escalate to.

### 9. Final cumulative-diff critic pass (multi-shortfall enhancements only)

When the enhancement is a single fix (one commit, ≤1 RFC section touched), the §7 per-fix critic pass IS the final gate. Skip this step.

When the enhancement is an iterative loop (multiple commits, multiple sections touched, OR any cross-section ripple), run one additional read-only critic against `git diff origin/main` for the whole branch BEFORE pushing. Same invariants as §7 plus: every commit cites a stable anchor in its body; the §Summary central claim is unchanged across the cumulative diff (not just per-commit); no body bytes change outside the sections the catalog said would be touched.

Empirical anchor: this runbook's PR #28 ran 5 RFC commits + 7 runbook commits and would have missed cumulative-diff drift (§Summary preservation across N commits, surplus sections touched) without the final-pass invocation.

### 10. One PR

The enhancement is one PR. PR title pattern:

- Edit: `docs(rfc-NNNN): <verb> <subsection> (post-<anchor>)` (e.g., `docs(rfc-0002): commit to dx-arch-meta as personal umbrella name`).
- Acceptance transition: `docs(rfc-NNNN,adr-NNNN): accept <title>` (the close-out includes the new ADR).

PR body cites the stable anchor that triggered the enhancement (sibling PR URL, resolved OQ, accepted ADR, new fact source).

## Example invocation prompt

The canonical iterative-loop invocation. Substitute `<RFC-NNNN-slug>` and `<short-topic>`; everything else is copy-paste.

```text
Run the how-to-enhance-existing-rfc runbook on content/rfc/<RFC-NNNN-slug>.md in ~/dx-arch-meta/repos/research-docs/. Iterate in a loop — catalog shortfalls (split non-deferred / deferred per runbook §2), fix one per commit, spawn one read-only critic per fix against §7 invariants, repeat until non-deferred catalog empty. Open ONE fresh PR for all the work.

Read first (in this order):
- content/runbooks/how-to-enhance-existing-rfc.md — the runbook you are executing.
- content/runbooks/how-to-author-rfc-from-scratch.md — sibling reference for vocabulary and PRIN-0001 escalation-surface discipline.
- content/rfc/_index.md — RFC status flow + conventions (draft / review mutable; accepted / rejected / withdrawn immutable).
- content/rfc/_template.md — RFC frontmatter schema (9 keys: id, title, status, date, author, tags, resolves-to, originating-oq, build). NEVER invent fields.
- content/open-questions/_template.md — OQ schema. Valid status: open | parked | promoted | dropped. NEVER use `resolved`.
- content/principles/0001-escalation-surface.md — PRIN-0001; typed surfaces for loose ends.

Verify location, branch, and target RFC status before any edit:

    git -C ~/dx-arch-meta/repos/research-docs fetch origin main
    pwd && git rev-parse --show-toplevel && git branch --show-current
    awk '/^status:/{print $2; exit}' content/rfc/<RFC-NNNN-slug>.md

HALT if status is accepted | rejected | withdrawn (runbook §Out of scope).

Cut a fresh branch from origin/main BEFORE any edit:

    git switch -c claude/enhance-rfc-<NNNN>-<short-topic> origin/main

Catalog at /tmp/<RFC-NNNN-slug>-shortfalls.md per runbook §2. Each non-deferred row needs a stable anchor (per §Pre-conditions, including the navigation-back-ref class). Deferred rows name the missing anchor in one sentence.

For each non-deferred row:
1. Apply discipline (append-only > surgical-correction > silent rewrite, per §4).
2. Run §5 ripple grep AFTER editing AND BEFORE `git add`.
3. Spawn caveman:cavecrew-reviewer with §7 invariants + the verbatim Location header from your UserPromptSubmit hook.
4. Fold BLOCK findings; commit with subject `docs(rfc-<NNNN>): <verb> <subsection> (post-<anchor>)` and body naming the shortfall # + anchor.

After the non-deferred catalog is empty: re-read the RFC end-to-end for newly-surfaced shortfalls; re-loop if any. Then per §9, run one final cumulative-diff critic on `git diff origin/main` before push.

Push and open ONE PR:

    git push -u origin claude/enhance-rfc-<NNNN>-<short-topic>
    gh pr create --head claude/enhance-rfc-<NNNN>-<short-topic> --base main \
      --title "docs(rfc-<NNNN>): <verb> per how-to-enhance-existing-rfc runbook" \
      --body "<sections: ## Summary / ## Initial catalog / ## Resolutions / ## Deferred shortfalls / ## Critic findings (cumulative-diff pass) / ## Test plan>"

Then invoke /run-pr-test-plan.

Hard constraints:
- ONE PR; ONE shortfall per commit.
- §Summary central claim immutable (if a fix would change it, halt — that's withdraw-and-fork).
- Frontmatter schema honored (9 RFC keys, 4 OQ status values); NEVER `status: resolved`, NEVER `parent-rfc:`, NEVER `originating-rfc:`.
- NEVER mutate accepted | rejected | withdrawn RFCs.
- If the loop exceeds ~12 iterations, halt and report — that signals withdraw-and-fork, not enhancement.
- Subagent invocations MUST include your UserPromptSubmit hook's verbatim Location header.
```

Empirical anchor: this is the prompt shape used to run PR #28 against RFC-0002 (5 RFC shortfalls + 7 runbook self-enhancements, including this §Example invocation prompt section).

## Expected outcome

- RFC at `content/rfc/NNNN-<slug>.md` updated; `status:` field unchanged unless the enhancement IS the transition.
- If close-out: `content/adr/NNNN-<slug>.md` exists; the RFC's `resolves-to:` set; §Open questions all resolved.
- Commit history reads as a trail of incremental, anchored additions — not silent rewrites.
- One PR, atomically capturing the edit + any escalation-surface updates.

## Rollback

`git revert` the enhancement commit if the change turns out to be wrong. Append-only discipline (Step 4) makes reverts surgically clean — the prior text is intact below the new content, not lost in a rewrite.

If the rollback reveals the underlying question is wrong (not just the edit): withdraw the RFC and open a new one. Don't try to back out incrementally — successive partial reverts is how RFCs end up mutated past recognition.

# How to audit loose ends

## When to run this

- Before opening a PR that touches `content/`.
- Before cutting a docs review session.
- On a `pre-push` hook (recommended cadence — no CI surface exists on this account).
- Ad hoc when triaging "what's unfinished?".

The audit operationalizes [PRIN-0001](/principles/0001-escalation-surface/) by reporting unresolved typed cross-references. See [methodology-unfinished-work](/design/methodology-unfinished-work/) for the full threading model.

## Pre-conditions

- Repository checked out at the branch you want to audit.
- Python 3.11+ on `PATH`.
- `PyYAML` installed (`pip install pyyaml` or pinned in a project-local virtualenv).
- Hugo extended on `PATH` (the audit shells out to Hugo for dangling-link detection — Hugo's `REF_NOT_FOUND` is the canonical source).
- `bin/audit-loose-ends.py` present *(separate PR — until then this runbook describes intent only).*

## Steps

1. From repo root:

    ```bash
    python3 bin/audit-loose-ends.py
    ```

   No flags = scan all of `content/`, all categories, report to stdout.

2. Read the report. Rows are formatted:

    ```
    content/adr/0042-foo.md:6 — Dangling — decided-from references RFC-0099 which does not exist
    content/benchmarks/api-latency.md:- — Stale — last run 2026-02-01 exceeds cadence "weekly"
    content/principles/0001-escalation-surface.md:- — Orphan principle — zero ADR citations in 90 days
    ```

3. For each row, choose one of:

   - **Resolve** — populate the missing cross-reference, ship the linked artifact, or rerun the benchmark.
   - **Drop** — if the loose end is no longer relevant, remove the typed field or transition the doc's status (e.g., `status: dropped` on an OQ with rationale in the body).
   - **Suppress** — only when there's a documented exception. Add to the doc:

       ```markdown
       <!-- audit-skip: <category> reason="<one sentence>" -->
       ```

       `<category>` must match the audit row's category (`pending`, `dangling`, `stale`, `orphan-principle`, `undefined-term`). `reason=` is mandatory.

4. Re-run the audit. If suppressed rows remain only in the **Suppressions in force** summary at the bottom, you're clean.

## Expected outcome

- Exit code `0` and an empty "Findings" section = no loose ends require action.
- Exit code `1` with findings rows = at least one typed loose end is unresolved and unsuppressed.
- Exit code `2` = audit itself errored (bad YAML, missing dependency, Hugo failed to build). Fix the tool problem, do not interpret as "clean".

## Rollback

Audit is read-only on `content/`. No rollback needed. If a `<!-- audit-skip: -->` marker was added by mistake, delete the comment.

## Common scenarios

### "Hugo emitted REF_NOT_FOUND but my frontmatter looks clean"

The audit defers all markdown-link integrity to Hugo. Fix the offending `{{</* ref */>}}` or relative link directly; the audit will turn green once Hugo does.

### "Authored a new ADR; decided-from rejects everything"

`decided-from:` accepts only `RFC-NNNN | EVAL-NNNN | OQ-NNNN`. If the ADR is genuinely original (no prior RFC / Eval / OQ), open a backfill OQ in the same PR and reference it — the methodology requires *some* traceable origin per [PRIN-0001](/principles/0001-escalation-surface/). The ADR-0000 meta-bootstrap is the only documented exception.

### "Glossary undefined-term flood"

Edit `content/glossary/allowlist.txt` (curated allowlist; see [OQ-0005](/open-questions/0005-glossary-granularity/) for the eventual replacement). If the allowlist itself is wrong, that's the fix — do not suppress per-doc.

# Should SWAF add a drift-surveillance pillar (or SU extension) to cover cadenced re-validation, aging signal, and failure catalog?

## The question

[SWAF](https://github.com/Wyatt-Rupp_prepass/dx-aicentral/tree/main/references/swaf) (the dx-aicentral Skill Well-Architected rubric) scores skills across 10 pillars: VA (Vertical Slice + Autonomy), OE (Operational Excellence), SE (Security), RE (Reliability), PE (Performance Efficiency), CO (Cost Optimization), SU (Sustainability), RI (Reasoning Integrity), CT (Controllability), CI (Context Integrity). All 10 measure properties of a skill **at delivery time**. None measure how the skill ages.

[skill-delivery-rigor §Tier 4](/design/skill-delivery-rigor/#tier-4-drift-surveillance) names three drift properties:

- **D4.1** — `/criteria-validate` re-fires on cadence (quarterly default); PASS → FAIL drift flagged.
- **D4.2** — Skill last-modified + last-eval-run dates queryable via aggregator (per [dx-aicentral-gap-audit #26](/notes/dx-aicentral-gap-audit/)).
- **D4.3** — `delivered → failed` flips emit structured failure-mode records suitable for cross-skill analysis (per [dx-aicentral-gap-audit #27](/notes/dx-aicentral-gap-audit/)).

These are explicitly out-of-scope for the current SWAF rubric and tagged `SWAF: —` in `skill-delivery-rigor`. The question this OQ holds: should they be upstreamed into SWAF so every skill (not just the 7-skill research pipeline) is scored on drift surveillance?

Two shapes for upstreaming:

1. **New pillar.** "DS — Drift Surveillance" as a new Tier-1 pillar with risk weighting comparable to OE. Three criteria (cadence, aging signal, failure catalog) mapped to D4.1/D4.2/D4.3.
2. **SU extension.** SU (Sustainability) currently covers maintainability, portability, ecosystem health — semantically adjacent to "the skill keeps working over time." Add SU-7/SU-8/SU-9 instead of a new pillar; preserves the 10-pillar count and avoids destabilizing existing scorecards.

## Why it matters

`/waf-skill-review` is now load-bearing in [how-to-deliver-a-skill-brief §step 9b](/runbooks/how-to-deliver-a-skill-brief/#9b-swaf-structural-quality-gate). If the rubric it scores against omits drift surveillance, every skill SWAF blesses will lack a drift surface unless the brief author remembers to add it manually. Drift omission is a known dx-aicentral gap (#26, #27); upstreaming closes it for *all* skills, not just pipeline ones.

Negative case: if drift surveillance is intrinsically per-skill-family (research-pipeline skills age differently than, say, `/onboard` or `/init`), forcing it into SWAF creates noise — a skill that has no meaningful "aging" signal would score badly on a criterion that doesn't apply. The SU-extension shape is more conservative here than a full new pillar.

## What's already been considered

- [skill-delivery-rigor §SWAF alignment](/design/skill-delivery-rigor/#swaf-alignment) — names the gap explicitly; tags D4.x with `SWAF: —` and points here.
- [dx-aicentral-gap-audit](/notes/dx-aicentral-gap-audit/) items #26 (aging signal) + #27 (structured failure catalog) — already filed as gaps in dx-aicentral but not as SWAF rubric extensions; they sit at the eval-harness / aggregator layer rather than the rubric layer.
- SWAF's existing 10-pillar layout has no currently-empty pillar slot — the OE pillar's "anticipate failure" principle is the closest semantic neighbor but its existing criteria all measure delivery-time properties (Step 0 validation, idempotence, structured reporting).
- [SWAF pillar-su.md](https://github.com/Wyatt-Rupp_prepass/dx-aicentral/blob/main/references/swaf/pillar-su.md) — "long-term maintainability, portability, ecosystem health" framing already adjacent; SU's current SU-1..SU-6 do not measure drift, but adding SU-7..SU-9 is a smaller change than a new pillar.

## What would unblock an RFC

1. After 2–3 pipeline skills ship and clear step 9 + step 9b in `how-to-deliver-a-skill-brief`, audit how often the D4.x items actually fire. If they catch real drift, the cost/benefit favors upstreaming. If they sit untriggered for a quarter, the upstream argument weakens.
2. Survey at least one non-pipeline dx-aicentral skill (e.g., `/onboard`, `/init`, a speckit command) for whether drift-surveillance would be load-bearing there. If not, the SU-extension framing is safer than a new pillar (so skills that don't need it just score N/A on SU-7..9 rather than failing a new Tier-1 pillar).
3. A worked SWAF scorecard prototype for one skill that includes the proposed criteria, generated by a forked `/waf-skill-review` with the candidate pillar/extension wired in. Concrete artifact, not prose.

Once that evidence exists, this OQ promotes to an ADR (decision: new pillar vs. SU extension vs. don't upstream) and an RFC against dx-aicentral that diffs `references/swaf/` per the chosen shape.

## State as of 2026-05-28

The first `unblock-by` precondition ("≥2 pipeline skills ship and clear step 9 + step 9b") is **met or exceeded**: the full 7-skill family (`/citation-detail-verify`, `/load-bearing-fullread`, `/source-recency-probe`, `/adversarial-frame`, `/survey-author`, `/criteria-validate`, `/invocation-discipline-lint`) is shipped and discoverable. The observation window opens now.

What remains is observation itself — quarterly tracking of whether D4.1/D4.2/D4.3 drift catches anything real on the shipped skills, plus the non-pipeline-skill probe (does drift surveillance apply to `/onboard` / `/init` / `/dev`?). The observation window's natural close date is **2026-08-28** (one quarter from substrate-complete). If by that date the D4.x items have either caught ≥1 real drift OR shown clear domain-applicability to non-pipeline skills, the OQ promotes to an RFC choosing between "new SWAF pillar" and "SU extension." If neither happens, the OQ stays parked until concrete drift evidence accumulates.

## State as of 2026-06-25 — cross-session-improvement survey as evidence base + scope extension

The survey [cross-session-improvement-heuristics](../survey/cross-session-improvement-heuristics.md) (merged #93) supplies the **theoretical grounding this OQ was missing**: it does not provide the empirical drift observation `unblock-by` #1 still requires (that remains an on-skill measurement, open until 2026-08-28), but it grounds *which* drift signals are worth scoring and how strong the evidence behind each is. The three Tier-4 items map cleanly:

- **D4.1 (cadenced re-validation)** ← what a re-fire *surfaces* is the strongest-evidenced keep-signal — a **shift in the failure-type distribution over a window** [A14]; *why* a cadence is needed is the SE/RCA "learning-to-change gap" — having a postmortem process does not by itself translate into improvement [A20].
- **D4.2 (aging signal)** ← forgetting/decay is a first-class memory dimension [A39], and forgetting failures (not recall failures) dominate on ForgetEval [A42] — a single-author 2026 benchmark whose "production" framing is the author's; field prevalence is unmeasured.
- **D4.3 (failure catalog)** ← the LLM/agent failure taxonomies that make failure machine-classifiable: MAST [A8], the SWE-agent taxonomy [A9], per-call tool-use error types [A11], with the honest caveat that auto-*attribution* of the decisive step is unreliable [A13] (a failure catalog can record categories cheaply; root-causing them is the hard part).

**Scope extension — the survey shows "cross-session readiness" is broader than drift.** Two axes the current OQ-0028 framing (drift/aging) does not cover, both of which a SWAF cross-session lens should also carry:

1. **External-signal / self-bias (→ RI).** A skill whose verification or improvement loop closes on its own judgement rather than an external/grounded signal is the survey's *strongest negative result* — intrinsic self-correction can degrade [A6] and self-refinement amplifies self-bias [A7]. This is a property of the skill's RI pillar (RI-5/RI-6), and the matching review-process question — should WAF scoring itself enforce author ≠ scorer — is filed separately as [OQ-0046](0046-waf-self-assessment-independent-scorer.md).
2. **Context hoarding (→ CI).** A skill that loads an ever-growing reference/memory footprint with no cap or eviction degrades by lost-in-the-middle / context-rot even when the relevant content is present [A34][A36][A37] — a CI-pillar concern.

So the pillar decision this OQ promotes to should be framed as **drift-surveillance ∪ external-signal-closure ∪ context-discipline = "SWAF cross-session readiness,"** not drift alone — while still leaving the new-pillar-vs-SU-extension shape open. The operational checklist that distills these signals (and maps each to RI/OE/SU/CI) now lives as a dx-aicentral reference, `references/cross-session-improvement-signals.md`, so a forked `/waf-skill-review` prototype (`unblock-by` #3) has concrete questions to wire in.
